faqs.question: I already speak English every day in Liberia. Why do I need this course?
faqs.answer: Liberian English is rich and expressive, but international examiners, universities, and employers expect formal standard English with different grammar, vocabulary, and tone. This course teaches you exactly where the two differ and how to switch confidently, without losing your own voice.

faqs.question: Will this course fully prepare me for the IELTS exam?
faqs.answer: It covers the complete IELTS foundation: format, band scoring, and strategies for all four papers, with extra depth on Writing Task 2 and Speaking. Combine it with the free official practice tests we link in each lesson, and most students are exam-ready in 6 to 10 weeks.

faqs.question: Do scholarships to India, Cyprus, and Turkey always require IELTS?
faqs.answer: Requirements vary. Some partner universities accept a WASSCE English pass or their own English interview, while others require IELTS 6.0 to 6.5. This course prepares you for all three paths, the test, the written application, and the interview, so no requirement catches you off guard.

faqs.question: Is the certificate useful if I stay and work in Liberia?
faqs.answer: Yes. Strong formal English is one of the most requested skills by employers and NGOs in Monrovia and across the counties. Your TIH certificate carries a unique verification code that Liberian employers can confirm instantly, and the email and interview skills apply to any job application at home.

Welcome to Complete English for Academic and Professional Success. This course is designed to help you use English clearly and confidently in school, at work, and in everyday life. Whether you are a student in Monrovia preparing for exams or a young professional applying for jobs, the skills you build here will open doors.

English is a shared language across West Africa, connecting people in classrooms, offices, and markets. Mastering it well gives you a strong voice in any room.

Key points

  • Purpose – build reading, writing, speaking, and listening for real academic and professional situations.
  • Progress – lessons move step by step from foundations to advanced use.
  • Practice – you learn by doing, not only by reading.

Example

Imagine writing a clear email to request an internship, then speaking confidently in the interview. By the end of this course, tasks like these will feel natural to you.

Why this matters

Strong English is a practical tool for success. It helps you pass exams, earn respect at work, and communicate across borders. Starting with a clear sense of purpose keeps you motivated through every lesson.

lessons.title: 1.2 Course Objectives
lessons.html:
📖 Course Objectives
Know exactly what you will achieve.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Course Objectives

Course Objectives is the focus of this Course Orientation lesson. It develops the learner's ability to begin the course with clear goals and an effective study routine.

learning objective

A clear statement of what a learner should know or do after instruction.

baseline

A starting level used to measure later progress.

study strategy

A deliberate method used to learn efficiently.

Course objectives are the clear goals that describe what you will be able to do by the end of your studies. They act like a map, showing where you are heading and how each lesson connects to your bigger success.

In this course, the objectives cover four language skills plus grammar, vocabulary, and confidence in real situations.

Key points

  • Communicate clearly – speak and write English that others understand easily.
  • Read with understanding – handle textbooks, reports, and articles.
  • Write with structure – produce organized essays, emails, and letters.
  • Grow vocabulary – use academic and professional words correctly.

Example

One objective is to write a formal application letter. After the relevant lessons, you should be able to draft a clean letter requesting a scholarship, with a proper greeting, body, and closing.

Why this matters

When you know the objectives, you can measure your own progress and stay focused. Employers and universities value people who can set clear goals and reach them. Understanding the destination helps you use every lesson wisely.

lessons.title: 1.3 Assessing Your English Level
lessons.html:
📖 Assessing Your English Level
Know where you stand before you climb.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Assessing Your English Level

Assessing Your English Level is the focus of this Course Orientation lesson. It develops the learner's ability to begin the course with clear goals and an effective study routine.

learning objective

A clear statement of what a learner should know or do after instruction.

baseline

A starting level used to measure later progress.

study strategy

A deliberate method used to learn efficiently.

Assessing your English level means honestly measuring your current skills in reading, writing, listening, and speaking. This helps you choose the right starting point and set realistic goals instead of guessing.

A common framework uses levels from beginner to advanced. Knowing your level tells you which areas need the most attention.

Key points

  • Self-assessment – reflect on what you can and cannot do yet.
  • Skill areas – check reading, writing, listening, and speaking separately.
  • Honesty – accurate answers give an accurate picture.

Example

Ask yourself: Can I read a newspaper article and understand the main idea? Can I write a short email without help? Can I follow a radio discussion? Answering yes or no to each shows your strengths and gaps clearly.

Why this matters

You cannot improve what you have not measured. A clear starting point saves time and builds confidence, because you focus effort where it counts. In academic and professional settings, knowing your true level helps you pick the right courses and describe your abilities honestly on a CV.

lessons.title: 1.4 Learning Strategies
lessons.html:
📖 Learning Strategies
Study smarter, not just harder.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Learning Strategies

Learning Strategies is the focus of this Course Orientation lesson. It develops the learner's ability to begin the course with clear goals and an effective study routine.

learning objective

A clear statement of what a learner should know or do after instruction.

baseline

A starting level used to measure later progress.

study strategy

A deliberate method used to learn efficiently.

Learning strategies are the practical methods you use to learn a language faster and remember it longer. Good strategies turn hours of study into real progress.

Everyone learns a little differently, but proven habits work for almost all learners.

Steps

  1. Set a small daily goal such as ten new words or one short reading.
  2. Practice actively by writing, speaking aloud, and testing yourself, not only re-reading.
  3. Use English daily through news, songs, or conversations with friends.
  4. Review regularly using spaced repetition so words stay in memory.
  5. Reflect weekly on what worked and adjust your plan.

Example

A student in Buchanan keeps a notebook, writes five new words each morning, uses them in sentences at lunch, and reviews them at night. In one month she has learned over one hundred useful words.

Why this matters

Strong strategies make learning steady and enjoyable rather than stressful. In school and at work, the ability to teach yourself new things is one of the most valuable skills you can own.

It replaces the need to study

questions.explanation: Self-monitoring helps learners notice what is working and adjust their approach accordingly.

lessons.title: 1.5 Academic vs. Professional English
lessons.html:
📖 Academic vs. Professional English
Same language, different purpose.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Academic vs. Professional English

Academic vs. Professional English is the focus of this Course Orientation lesson. It develops the learner's ability to begin the course with clear goals and an effective study routine.

learning objective

A clear statement of what a learner should know or do after instruction.

baseline

A starting level used to measure later progress.

study strategy

A deliberate method used to learn efficiently.

Academic English is the formal style used in schools and universities, in essays, exams, and research. Professional English is the style used in the workplace, in emails, reports, meetings, and interviews. Both are formal, but they serve different goals.

Academic English explains and argues ideas carefully. Professional English gets work done clearly and politely.

Key points

  • Academic English – uses evidence, references, and analysis; longer, careful sentences.
  • Professional English – uses direct, action-focused language; short and courteous.
  • Shared base – both avoid slang and value correct grammar.

Example

Academic: The data suggest that rainfall significantly affects crop yields in the region. Professional: Please find attached the crop report; let me know if you need anything else before Friday.

Why this matters

Using the right style at the right time shows maturity and respect. A student who writes an essay like a text message loses marks, and a worker who writes an email like an essay wastes time. Knowing the difference helps you succeed in both worlds.

lessons.title: 1.6 Setting Language Goals
lessons.html:
📖 Setting Language Goals
A clear target pulls you forward.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Setting Language Goals

Setting Language Goals is the focus of this Course Orientation lesson. It develops the learner's ability to begin the course with clear goals and an effective study routine.

learning objective

A clear statement of what a learner should know or do after instruction.

baseline

A starting level used to measure later progress.

study strategy

A deliberate method used to learn efficiently.

Setting language goals means deciding clearly what you want to achieve in English and by when. Good goals are specific and measurable, so you know when you have reached them.

Vague wishes like get better rarely lead to action. Clear goals do.

Steps

  1. Choose a clear outcome such as write a job application without help.
  2. Make it measurable by adding numbers, like learn 300 professional words.
  3. Set a deadline such as within three months.
  4. Break it down into weekly mini-goals.
  5. Track progress and celebrate each small win.

Example

Weak goal: I want to speak better English. Strong goal: In two months I will hold a five-minute conversation about my studies with correct grammar, practising three times a week.

Why this matters

Clear goals keep you motivated and let you measure real growth. Universities and employers respect people who set targets and reach them. When your goals are sharp, every study session has a purpose.

lessons.title: 1.7 Study Plan
lessons.html:
📖 Study Plan
Turn your goals into a weekly routine.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Study Plan

Study Plan is the focus of this Course Orientation lesson. It develops the learner's ability to begin the course with clear goals and an effective study routine.

learning objective

A clear statement of what a learner should know or do after instruction.

baseline

A starting level used to measure later progress.

study strategy

A deliberate method used to learn efficiently.

A study plan is a written schedule that shows when, what, and how you will study. It changes good intentions into real action by giving each week a clear structure.

Even fifteen focused minutes a day adds up quickly when it is planned.

Steps

  1. Check your time and pick fixed study slots, even short ones.
  2. Balance the skills across reading, writing, listening, speaking, and vocabulary.
  3. Assign tasks to days, for example vocabulary on Monday, writing on Wednesday.
  4. Include review time at the end of each week.
  5. Be realistic so the plan fits your real life and you can keep it.

Example

A trader in Ganta studies before opening his shop: Monday and Thursday for new words, Tuesday and Friday for reading news aloud, Saturday for writing a short paragraph. Sunday he reviews the week.

Why this matters

A plan removes the daily question of what should I study and replaces it with action. This discipline mirrors the time-management skills valued in every school and workplace, helping you achieve steady, lasting progress.

lessons.title: 2.1 Parts of Speech
lessons.html:
📖 Parts of Speech
Every word in English has a job to do.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Parts of Speech

Parts of Speech is the focus of this English Grammar Fundamentals lesson. It develops the learner's ability to construct accurate Standard English sentences.

grammar rule

A convention governing how words and clauses form sentences.

accuracy

Correct use of language forms and conventions.

sentence pattern

An organized grammatical arrangement of words and clauses.

The parts of speech are the eight basic categories that describe how a word functions in a sentence: nouns, pronouns, verbs, adjectives, adverbs, prepositions, conjunctions, and interjections. The same word can change category depending on how it is used, so we look at its job in the sentence, not the word alone.

Knowing these categories helps you build correct sentences and understand grammar rules that follow.

Key points

  • Noun – names a person, place, thing, or idea (Monrovia, teacher, hope).
  • Verb – shows action or a state of being (write, is).
  • Adjective – describes a noun (a busy market).
  • Adverb – describes a verb, adjective, or adverb (she spoke clearly).
  • Pronoun, preposition, conjunction, interjection – replace nouns, show relationships, join ideas, or show feeling.

Example

The diligent student (adjective + noun) quickly (adverb) submitted (verb) her (pronoun) report to (preposition) the office, and (conjunction) everyone applauded.

Why this matters

When you can name the job each word does, you can spot errors, follow grammar rules, and build clear, professional sentences for essays, reports, and presentations.

lessons.title: 2.2 Sentence Structure
lessons.html:
📖 Sentence Structure
A good sentence has a solid skeleton.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Sentence Structure

Sentence Structure is the focus of this English Grammar Fundamentals lesson. It develops the learner's ability to construct accurate Standard English sentences.

grammar rule

A convention governing how words and clauses form sentences.

accuracy

Correct use of language forms and conventions.

sentence pattern

An organized grammatical arrangement of words and clauses.

Sentence structure is the way words are arranged into meaningful units. Every complete sentence needs a subject (who or what) and a predicate (what the subject does or is). English also arranges ideas into four sentence types: simple, compound, complex, and compound-complex.

Varying your structure keeps writing lively and shows control of ideas.

Key points

  • Simple – one independent clause (The market opens early.).
  • Compound – two independent clauses joined by a conjunction (She studied, and she passed.).
  • Complex – one independent and one dependent clause (Because it rained, class was late.).
  • Compound-complex – two independent clauses plus at least one dependent clause.

Example

Simple: The farmer harvested the rice. Compound: The farmer harvested the rice, and his wife sold it. Complex: When the rains ended, the farmer harvested the rice.

Why this matters

Clear structure helps readers follow your point in essays and workplace emails. Mixing sentence types makes your writing mature and easy to understand, which matters in exams and professional reports.

lessons.title: 2.3 Nouns
lessons.html:
📖 Nouns
Nouns are the names we give to the world.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Nouns

Nouns is the focus of this English Grammar Fundamentals lesson. It develops the learner's ability to construct accurate Standard English sentences.

grammar rule

A convention governing how words and clauses form sentences.

accuracy

Correct use of language forms and conventions.

sentence pattern

An organized grammatical arrangement of words and clauses.

A noun names a person, place, thing, or idea. Nouns can be common (city) or proper (Monrovia), concrete (chair) or abstract (freedom), countable (books) or uncountable (water). They can act as subjects, objects, or complements in a sentence.

Nouns also show number (singular or plural) and can be possessive.

Key points

  • Common vs proper – proper nouns name specific people or places and take a capital letter (Liberia, Grace).
  • Countable vs uncountable – countable nouns have plurals (one mango, two mangoes); uncountable ones do not (advice, rice).
  • Abstract – names ideas or feelings you cannot touch (courage, education).
  • Possessive – shows ownership with an apostrophe (the teacher's desk).

Example

Grace (proper noun) bought three baskets (countable) of cassava (uncountable) at the market, and her honesty (abstract) impressed the trader.

Why this matters

Choosing the right noun form keeps your writing accurate. Knowing countable and uncountable nouns prevents errors like 'many informations', which is common but wrong, and helps you write polished academic and business English.

lessons.title: 2.4 Pronouns
lessons.html:
📖 Pronouns
Small words that save us from repeating names.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Pronouns

Pronouns is the focus of this English Grammar Fundamentals lesson. It develops the learner's ability to construct accurate Standard English sentences.

grammar rule

A convention governing how words and clauses form sentences.

accuracy

Correct use of language forms and conventions.

sentence pattern

An organized grammatical arrangement of words and clauses.

A pronoun is a word that takes the place of a noun so we do not repeat it again and again. Instead of saying 'Musu said Musu was tired', we say 'Musu said she was tired'. The noun a pronoun replaces is called its antecedent.

Pronouns must agree with their antecedent in number and gender.

Key points

  • Personal – I, you, he, she, it, we, they and their object forms (me, him, them).
  • Possessive – mine, yours, his, hers, ours, theirs.
  • Relative – who, whom, which, that link clauses.
  • Reflexive – myself, herself, themselves refer back to the subject.

Example

The students finished their exam, and they were proud of themselves because the results belonged to them alone.

Why this matters

Correct pronoun use keeps writing smooth and avoids confusion about who did what. In reports and essays, clear pronoun-antecedent agreement makes your meaning easy to follow and shows careful, professional command of English.

lessons.title: 📝 Practice: Pronouns
lessons.html: Quick check: Review the notes and complete the two exercises, then answer these to confirm you understood Pronouns.

lessons.title: 2.5 Verbs
lessons.html:
📖 Verbs
The engine of every sentence.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Verbs

Verbs is the focus of this English Grammar Fundamentals lesson. It develops the learner's ability to construct accurate Standard English sentences.

grammar rule

A convention governing how words and clauses form sentences.

accuracy

Correct use of language forms and conventions.

sentence pattern

An organized grammatical arrangement of words and clauses.

A verb expresses an action (run, write, build) or a state of being (is, seem, become). Every complete sentence needs at least one verb. Verbs change form to show tense, number, and person, and they can be main verbs or helping (auxiliary) verbs.

Some verbs are transitive (they take an object) and some are intransitive (they do not).

Key points

  • Action verbs – show what the subject does (she teaches, they trade).
  • Linking verbs – connect the subject to a description (he is a nurse, it seems fair).
  • Helping verbs – support the main verb (have, be, do, will).
  • Transitive vs intransitive – transitive verbs need an object (She sells fish); intransitive do not (The baby slept).

Example

The nurse checked (action) the patients, was (linking) calm, and had (helping) prepared the medicine before the doctor arrived.

Why this matters

Strong, precise verbs make writing clear and forceful. Choosing exact verbs instead of vague ones ('improve' rather than 'make better') strengthens essays, proposals, and workplace communication.

lessons.html: Quick check: Review the notes and complete the two exercises, then answer these to confirm you understood Verbs.

questions.explanation: 'Designed' expresses the action performed by the subject.

questions.explanation: 'Have' assists the main verb 'finished', so it is the helping (auxiliary) verb.

lessons.title: 2.6 Verb Tenses
lessons.html:
📖 Verb Tenses
Tenses tell us when something happens.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Verb Tenses

Verb Tenses is the focus of this English Grammar Fundamentals lesson. It develops the learner's ability to construct accurate Standard English sentences.

grammar rule

A convention governing how words and clauses form sentences.

accuracy

Correct use of language forms and conventions.

sentence pattern

An organized grammatical arrangement of words and clauses.

Tense is the form of a verb that shows time: past, present, or future. Each of these has simple, continuous, perfect, and perfect continuous forms, giving twelve tenses in all. Using the right tense makes your timeline of events clear to the reader.

Keep tenses consistent unless the time genuinely changes.

Key points

  • Simple – general facts or habits (I work).
  • Continuous – action in progress (I am working).
  • Perfect – action completed with a link to now (I have worked).
  • Perfect continuous – ongoing action up to a point (I have been working).

Example

Present simple: Kollie studies at the university. Past simple: Kollie studied last night. Future simple: Kollie will study tomorrow. Present continuous: Kollie is studying now. Present perfect: Kollie has studied for three years.

Why this matters

Accurate tenses tell your reader exactly when things happen. In academic writing and reports, consistent tense keeps your account clear and professional, and avoids confusing your examiner or manager.

lessons.title: 📝 Practice: Verb Tenses
lessons.html: Quick check: Review the notes and complete the two exercises, then answer these to confirm you understood Verb Tenses.

questions.question: Which sentence is in the present perfect tense?
questions.explanation: 'Have written' uses 'have' plus a past participle, forming the present perfect.

questions.question: Which verb form correctly completes 'While I ___ dinner, the phone rang'?
questions.explanation: 'Was cooking' describes an ongoing past action, the past continuous tense.

questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses the future perfect tense?
options: By 2030, they will have completed the plan.
questions.explanation: 'Will have completed' expresses an action finished before a future point, the future perfect.

lessons.title: 2.7 Subject-Verb Agreement
lessons.html:
📖 Subject-Verb Agreement
Subjects and verbs must match in number.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Subject-Verb Agreement

Subject-Verb Agreement is the focus of this English Grammar Fundamentals lesson. It develops the learner's ability to construct accurate Standard English sentences.

grammar rule

A convention governing how words and clauses form sentences.

accuracy

Correct use of language forms and conventions.

sentence pattern

An organized grammatical arrangement of words and clauses.

Subject-verb agreement means the verb must match its subject in number and person. A singular subject takes a singular verb, and a plural subject takes a plural verb. The tricky part is finding the true subject, especially when other words come between it and the verb.

In the present tense, most singular subjects add an -s to the verb.

Key points

  • Singular subject, singular verb – The boy runs. The boys run.
  • Watch for phrases in between – The basket of mangoes is heavy (subject is basket).
  • Compound subjects with 'and' – usually plural (Musu and Kollie are here).
  • Each, everyone, nobody – take a singular verb (Everyone is welcome).

Example

The list of approved candidates was posted yesterday. (The subject is 'list', which is singular, so the verb is 'was', not 'were'.)

Why this matters

Agreement errors are among the most noticed mistakes in writing. Getting it right signals careful, educated English and keeps examiners and employers focused on your ideas rather than your errors.

lessons.title: 📝 Practice: Subject-Verb Agreement
lessons.html: Quick check: Review the notes and complete the two exercises, then answer these to confirm you understood Subject-Verb Agreement.

questions.question: Which sentence has correct subject-verb agreement?
options: The list of items is long.
The list of items were long.
The list of items are long.
The list of items be long.
questions.explanation: The subject 'list' is singular, so it takes the singular verb 'is'.

questions.explanation: With 'neither...nor', the verb agrees with the nearer subject 'students', so 'are' is correct.

questions.question: Which verb correctly completes 'Each of the employees ___ a badge'?
questions.explanation: 'Each' is singular and takes the singular verb 'has'.

lessons.title: 2.8 Adjectives
lessons.html:
📖 Adjectives
Words that add colour and detail.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Adjectives

Adjectives is the focus of this English Grammar Fundamentals lesson. It develops the learner's ability to construct accurate Standard English sentences.

grammar rule

A convention governing how words and clauses form sentences.

accuracy

Correct use of language forms and conventions.

sentence pattern

An organized grammatical arrangement of words and clauses.

An adjective describes or modifies a noun or pronoun, telling us which one, what kind, how many, or whose. Adjectives make writing vivid and precise: a market becomes 'a crowded, noisy market'. They usually come before the noun or after a linking verb.

Adjectives can also compare things using comparative and superlative forms.

Key points

  • Descriptive – give quality (a tall building, fresh fish).
  • Comparative – compare two things (taller, more careful).
  • Superlative – compare three or more (tallest, most careful).
  • Order – opinion before size before colour (a lovely small blue bag).

Example

The diligent student wrote a clear, well-organised essay that was better than her last one and the best in the class.

Why this matters

Well-chosen adjectives make descriptions precise and persuasive, which helps in academic writing and in professional documents like proposals. But use them wisely; too many adjectives weaken your point rather than strengthen it.

lessons.title: 📝 Practice: Adjectives
lessons.html: Quick check: Review the notes and complete the two exercises, then answer these to confirm you understood Adjectives.

questions.question: Which word is an adjective in 'The tall building collapsed'?
questions.explanation: 'Tall' describes the noun 'building', making it an adjective.

questions.question: Which word correctly completes the comparative 'This test is ___ than the last one'?
questions.explanation: Longer adjectives form the comparative with 'more', giving 'more difficult'.

questions.question: Which sentence orders its adjectives correctly?
questions.explanation: Size comes before color in English adjective order, so 'big red car' is correct.

lessons.title: 2.9 Adverbs
lessons.html:
📖 Adverbs
They tell us how, when, where, and how often.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Adverbs

Adverbs is the focus of this English Grammar Fundamentals lesson. It develops the learner's ability to construct accurate Standard English sentences.

grammar rule

A convention governing how words and clauses form sentences.

accuracy

Correct use of language forms and conventions.

sentence pattern

An organized grammatical arrangement of words and clauses.

An adverb modifies a verb, an adjective, or another adverb. It answers questions such as how, when, where, how often, and to what degree. Many adverbs end in -ly (quickly, carefully), but common ones like often, here, and very do not.

Adverbs add precision to actions and descriptions.

Key points

  • Manner – how something happens (She spoke calmly).
  • Time – when (He arrived yesterday).
  • Place – where (They waited outside).
  • Frequency and degree – how often or how much (always, very, quite).

Example

The chairperson carefully (manner) explained the plan yesterday (time) and everyone listened very (degree) attentively.

Why this matters

Adverbs sharpen meaning and tone in speaking and writing. Placing them correctly, and not overusing them, keeps your sentences precise and professional, whether you are answering an exam question or giving a workplace update.

lessons.title: 📝 Practice: Adverbs
lessons.html: Quick check: Review the notes and complete the two exercises, then answer these to confirm you understood Adverbs.

questions.question: Which word is an adverb in 'He spoke very softly'?
questions.explanation: 'Softly' modifies the verb 'spoke', making it an adverb.

questions.question: Which sentence uses an adverb of frequency correctly?
questions.explanation: Adverbs of frequency come after the verb 'be', so 'is always late' is correct.

questions.question: In 'The team performed well', what does 'well' describe?
questions.explanation: 'Well' is an adverb describing how the team performed.

lessons.title: 2.10 Articles
lessons.html:
📖 Articles
The small words 'a', 'an', and 'the' matter more than you think.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Articles

Articles is the focus of this English Grammar Fundamentals lesson. It develops the learner's ability to construct accurate Standard English sentences.

grammar rule

A convention governing how words and clauses form sentences.

accuracy

Correct use of language forms and conventions.

sentence pattern

An organized grammatical arrangement of words and clauses.

Articles are special adjectives that come before nouns. English has two kinds: the indefinite articles 'a' and 'an', used for one unspecified thing, and the definite article 'the', used for a specific thing already known to the listener. Some nouns need no article at all.

Use 'a' before consonant sounds and 'an' before vowel sounds.

Key points

  • a / an – introduce something for the first time (I saw a dog).
  • the – refer to a specific, known thing (The dog was mine).
  • Sound, not letter – an hour, a university (we listen to the sound).
  • Zero article – with most plurals and uncountables in general (Water is life).

Example

I bought a book at the market. The book is about the history of Liberia. It took me an hour to read.

Why this matters

Articles are easy to drop in speech but noticeable when missing in writing. Using them correctly makes your English sound natural and polished in essays, applications, and professional emails.

lessons.title: 📝 Practice: Articles
lessons.html: Quick check: Review the notes and complete the two exercises, then answer these to confirm you understood Articles.

questions.question: Which article correctly completes 'She is ___ honest person'?
questions.explanation: 'Honest' begins with a vowel sound, so 'an' is used.

questions.question: Which sentence uses articles correctly?
options: I saw the elephant at a zoo.
I saw a elephant at the zoo.
I saw an elephant at the zoo.
questions.explanation: 'An' precedes the vowel sound in 'elephant', and 'the' identifies the specific zoo.

questions.question: When do we typically use the definite article 'the'?
options: When referring to a specific, known thing
questions.explanation: 'The' is used when the noun refers to something specific and identifiable.

lessons.title: 2.11 Prepositions
lessons.html:
📖 Prepositions
Little words that show relationships.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Prepositions

Prepositions is the focus of this English Grammar Fundamentals lesson. It develops the learner's ability to construct accurate Standard English sentences.

grammar rule

A convention governing how words and clauses form sentences.

accuracy

Correct use of language forms and conventions.

sentence pattern

An organized grammatical arrangement of words and clauses.

A preposition links a noun or pronoun to another word, showing relationships of place, time, direction, or manner: in, on, at, under, before, with, and many more. A preposition plus its noun forms a prepositional phrase (on the table, after the meeting).

English prepositions often go with particular verbs and expressions, so they are learned partly by practice.

Key points

  • Place – in, on, at, under, between (the keys are on the desk).
  • Time – at, on, in, before, during (at noon, on Monday, in July).
  • Direction – to, into, from, towards (she walked to school).
  • Fixed pairs – depend on, interested in, good at.

Example

The meeting is at nine on Monday in the main hall, and it depends on the manager's arrival from Buchanan.

Why this matters

Prepositions are a frequent source of errors for English learners. Using them correctly, especially in fixed expressions, makes your writing and speech sound natural and confident in study and at work.

lessons.title: 📝 Practice: Prepositions
lessons.html: Quick check: Review the notes and complete the two exercises, then answer these to confirm you understood Prepositions.

questions.question: Which preposition correctly completes 'The meeting is ___ Monday'?
questions.explanation: We use 'on' with days of the week.

questions.question: Which sentence uses the preposition of time correctly?
questions.explanation: We use 'at' with specific clock times.

questions.question: Which preposition best completes 'The keys are ___ the drawer'?
questions.explanation: 'In' indicates something enclosed inside the drawer.

lessons.title: 2.12 Conjunctions
lessons.html:
📖 Conjunctions
The joiners that connect ideas.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Conjunctions

Conjunctions is the focus of this English Grammar Fundamentals lesson. It develops the learner's ability to construct accurate Standard English sentences.

grammar rule

A convention governing how words and clauses form sentences.

accuracy

Correct use of language forms and conventions.

sentence pattern

An organized grammatical arrangement of words and clauses.

A conjunction joins words, phrases, or clauses. Coordinating conjunctions link equal parts, subordinating conjunctions attach a dependent clause to a main one, and correlative conjunctions work in pairs. Conjunctions let you combine short sentences into smoother, more mature ones.

Remember the coordinating conjunctions with the word FANBOYS: for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so.

Key points

  • Coordinating – join equals (bread and butter; tired but happy).
  • Subordinating – show reason, time, condition (because, when, although, if).
  • Correlative – used in pairs (either...or, not only...but also).
  • Punctuation – use a comma before a coordinating conjunction joining two full sentences.

Example

Although the road was bad, the driver arrived on time, and not only the passengers but also the goods were safe.

Why this matters

Conjunctions let you connect ideas logically instead of writing choppy, disconnected sentences. This is essential for clear arguments in essays and for professional reports where ideas must flow smoothly.

lessons.title: 📝 Practice: Conjunctions
lessons.html: Quick check: Review the notes and complete the two exercises, then answer these to confirm you understood Conjunctions.

questions.question: Which word is a coordinating conjunction?
questions.explanation: 'But' is a coordinating conjunction that joins equal elements.

questions.question: Which subordinating conjunction correctly completes '___ it was raining, we stayed home'?
questions.explanation: 'Because' introduces a reason in a dependent clause.

questions.question: Which sentence uses a correlative conjunction pair correctly?
options: Both you or I can attend.
questions.explanation: 'Either...or' is the correct correlative conjunction pair.

lessons.title: 2.13 Modals
lessons.html:
📖 Modals
Verbs that express possibility, permission, and obligation.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Modals

Modals is the focus of this English Grammar Fundamentals lesson. It develops the learner's ability to construct accurate Standard English sentences.

grammar rule

A convention governing how words and clauses form sentences.

accuracy

Correct use of language forms and conventions.

sentence pattern

An organized grammatical arrangement of words and clauses.

Modal verbs are helping verbs such as can, could, may, might, must, shall, should, will, and would. They express ideas like ability, permission, possibility, necessity, and advice. Modals are always followed by the base form of the main verb and never change form to add -s.

They also help us sound polite and appropriately formal.

Key points

  • Ability – can, could (She can drive).
  • Permission / politeness – may, could, would (May I come in?).
  • Obligation / necessity – must, have to, should (You must submit it today).
  • Possibility – may, might, could (It might rain).

Example

Applicants must attach their certificates, and they should arrive early. If you have a question, you may call the office, and we will help you.

Why this matters

Modals control tone and degree of certainty. Choosing 'could you' instead of a bare command makes requests polite, and 'must' versus 'should' shows how strong a rule is, which matters greatly in professional emails and formal writing.

lessons.title: 📝 Practice: Modals
lessons.html: Quick check: Review the notes and complete the two exercises, then answer these to confirm you understood Modals.

questions.question: Which modal expresses strong obligation?
questions.explanation: 'Must' expresses strong obligation or necessity.

questions.question: Which modal correctly completes 'You ___ smoke here; it is prohibited'?
questions.explanation: 'Must not' expresses prohibition.

questions.question: Which sentence uses a modal to express polite permission?
questions.explanation: 'May I' is a polite way to ask for permission.

lessons.title: 2.14 Active & Passive Voice
lessons.html:
📖 Active & Passive Voice
Who is doing the action, and does it matter?

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Active & Passive Voice

Active & Passive Voice is the focus of this English Grammar Fundamentals lesson. It develops the learner's ability to construct accurate Standard English sentences.

grammar rule

A convention governing how words and clauses form sentences.

accuracy

Correct use of language forms and conventions.

sentence pattern

An organized grammatical arrangement of words and clauses.

In the active voice, the subject does the action: 'The manager wrote the report.' In the passive voice, the subject receives the action: 'The report was written by the manager.' The passive is formed with a form of 'be' plus the past participle, and the doer can be dropped or added with 'by'.

Active voice is usually clearer and stronger; passive is useful when the doer is unknown or unimportant.

Key points

  • Active – subject performs the action; direct and vigorous.
  • Passive – subject receives the action; formed with be + past participle.
  • Use passive – when the doer is unknown or the action matters more (The bridge was destroyed).
  • Prefer active – for clear, lively writing in most cases.

Example

Active: The committee approved the budget. Passive: The budget was approved by the committee. Passive without doer: The budget was approved yesterday.

Why this matters

Knowing both voices lets you choose the right emphasis. Reports and scientific writing often use the passive, while clear business and academic prose usually prefers the active for directness and energy.

lessons.html: Quick check: Review the notes and complete the two exercises, then answer these to confirm you understood Active & Passive Voice.

questions.question: Which sentence is written in the passive voice?
options: The meal was cooked by the chef.
questions.explanation: The subject 'meal' receives the action, and 'was cooked' shows passive voice.

questions.question: Which is the correct passive form of 'The company launched a new product'?
options: The company was launched a product.
A new product launched the company.
A new product was launched by the company.
A new product launches the company.
questions.explanation: The object becomes the subject and the verb becomes 'was launched by the company'.

questions.question: Which is the correct active-voice version of 'The letter was written by Sara'?
questions.explanation: In the active voice, the doer 'Sara' becomes the subject: 'Sara wrote the letter'.

lessons.title: 2.15 Direct & Indirect Speech
lessons.html:
📖 Direct & Indirect Speech
Two ways to report what someone said.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Direct & Indirect Speech

Direct & Indirect Speech is the focus of this English Grammar Fundamentals lesson. It develops the learner's ability to construct accurate Standard English sentences.

grammar rule

A convention governing how words and clauses form sentences.

accuracy

Correct use of language forms and conventions.

sentence pattern

An organized grammatical arrangement of words and clauses.

Direct speech quotes a person's exact words inside quotation marks: She said, 'I am tired.' Indirect (reported) speech tells what was said without the exact words and usually without quotation marks: She said that she was tired. When we report, tenses, pronouns, and time words often shift back.

The verb 'said' is common, but 'told', 'asked', and 'explained' are also useful.

Key points

  • Direct – exact words in quotation marks (He said, 'I will come.').
  • Indirect – reported words, often with 'that' (He said that he would come).
  • Tense shift – present becomes past (am becomes was, will becomes would).
  • Time and pronouns change – today becomes that day; I becomes he or she.

Example

Direct: The teacher said, 'You must submit your work tomorrow.' Indirect: The teacher said that we had to submit our work the next day.

Why this matters

Reporting speech accurately is vital in essays, journalism, and workplace summaries of meetings. Handling the tense and pronoun shifts correctly shows control and keeps your reports faithful to what was actually said.

lessons.title: 📝 Practice: Direct & Indirect Speech
lessons.html: Quick check: Review the notes and complete the two exercises, then answer these to confirm you understood Direct & Indirect Speech.

questions.question: Which is the correct indirect speech for She said, 'I am tired'?
options: She said that she was tired.
She said that she is tired.
questions.explanation: In reported speech, present tense shifts to past, giving 'she was tired'.

questions.question: Which is the correct direct speech form?
options: He said that he was busy.
questions.explanation: Direct speech quotes the exact words within quotation marks.

questions.question: Which correctly reports the question He asked, 'Where do you live'?
options: He asked where do you live.
He asked where did I live.
questions.explanation: Reported questions use statement word order and shift tense, giving 'where I lived'.

lessons.title: 2.16 Conditionals
lessons.html:
📖 Conditionals
Talking about 'if' and its results.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Conditionals

Conditionals is the focus of this English Grammar Fundamentals lesson. It develops the learner's ability to construct accurate Standard English sentences.

grammar rule

A convention governing how words and clauses form sentences.

accuracy

Correct use of language forms and conventions.

sentence pattern

An organized grammatical arrangement of words and clauses.

Conditional sentences describe a condition and its result, usually using 'if'. English has four main types that express situations from certain facts to impossible imagined pasts. Each type uses a particular pattern of tenses in the 'if' clause and the result clause.

Learning the patterns lets you talk clearly about cause, possibility, and regret.

Key points

  • Zero – facts always true (If you heat water, it boils).
  • First – likely future (If it rains, we will stay home).
  • Second – unlikely or imagined present (If I had money, I would travel).
  • Third – impossible past, often regret (If I had studied, I would have passed).

Example

First: If the loan is approved, she will expand her shop. Second: If she were the mayor, she would fix the roads. Third: If they had left earlier, they would have caught the bus.

Why this matters

Conditionals let you reason about consequences, make plans, give advice, and reflect on choices. These skills are essential for persuasive essays, business proposals, and clear problem-solving discussions at work.

lessons.html: Quick check: Review the notes and complete the two exercises, then answer these to confirm you understood Conditionals.

questions.question: Which verb form correctly completes the first conditional 'If it rains, we ___ the trip'?
questions.explanation: The first conditional uses 'will' plus the base verb in the result clause.

options: If I had money, I would travel.
If I have money, I would travel.
If I had money, I will travel.
If I have money, I travelled.
questions.explanation: The second conditional uses past simple in the 'if' clause and 'would' in the result.

questions.question: Which verb form completes the third conditional 'If she had studied, she ___ the exam'?
questions.explanation: The third conditional uses 'would have' plus a past participle for unreal past results.

lessons.title: 2.17 Relative Clauses
lessons.html:
📖 Relative Clauses
Adding extra detail without starting a new sentence.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Relative Clauses

Relative Clauses is the focus of this English Grammar Fundamentals lesson. It develops the learner's ability to construct accurate Standard English sentences.

grammar rule

A convention governing how words and clauses form sentences.

accuracy

Correct use of language forms and conventions.

sentence pattern

An organized grammatical arrangement of words and clauses.

A relative clause gives more information about a noun. It begins with a relative pronoun such as who, whom, whose, which, or that. Defining (restrictive) clauses give essential information and take no commas; non-defining clauses add extra, non-essential detail and are set off by commas.

Use 'who' for people, 'which' for things, and 'that' for either in defining clauses.

Key points

  • Defining – essential, no commas (The student who won lives in Gbarnga).
  • Non-defining – extra detail, with commas (My uncle, who lives in Kakata, is a farmer).
  • who / whom / whose – for people and possession.
  • which / that – for things; 'that' is not used in non-defining clauses.

Example

The report that she submitted was excellent. The manager, who joined last year, praised it. The office, which is new, was full.

Why this matters

Relative clauses let you combine ideas smoothly and add precise detail, making your writing more sophisticated. Knowing when to use commas also prevents changing your meaning, which is important in careful academic and professional writing.

lessons.title: 📝 Practice: Relative Clauses
lessons.html: Quick check: Review the notes and complete the two exercises, then answer these to confirm you understood Relative Clauses.

questions.question: Which relative pronoun correctly completes 'The woman ___ called you is my aunt'?
questions.explanation: 'Who' refers to people acting as the subject of the clause.

questions.question: Which sentence uses a relative clause correctly?
options: The book who I read was long.
The book whose I read was long.
The book where I read was long.
The book which I read was long.
questions.explanation: 'Which' refers to things such as 'the book'.

questions.question: Which relative pronoun shows possession in 'The man ___ car was stolen called the police'?
questions.explanation: 'Whose' indicates possession, referring to the man's car.

lessons.title: 2.18 Punctuation
lessons.html:
📖 Punctuation
The traffic signals of writing.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Punctuation

Punctuation is the focus of this English Grammar Fundamentals lesson. It develops the learner's ability to construct accurate Standard English sentences.

grammar rule

A convention governing how words and clauses form sentences.

accuracy

Correct use of language forms and conventions.

sentence pattern

An organized grammatical arrangement of words and clauses.

Punctuation marks guide the reader through your sentences, showing where to pause, stop, or emphasise. Correct punctuation prevents confusion and can completely change meaning. The main marks are the full stop, comma, question mark, exclamation mark, apostrophe, colon, semicolon, and quotation marks.

Even a single comma can change what a sentence means.

Key points

  • Full stop – ends a statement.
  • Comma – separates items and clauses and marks short pauses.
  • Apostrophe – shows possession (Grace's book) or contraction (don't).
  • Colon and semicolon – introduce lists or join related sentences.

Example

Compare: 'Let's eat, Grandma.' and 'Let's eat Grandma.' The comma decides whether we invite Grandma to eat or plan to eat her.

Why this matters

Good punctuation makes your meaning clear and your writing professional. In exams, applications, and workplace documents, careful punctuation shows attention to detail and helps readers understand you the first time.

lessons.title: 📝 Practice: Punctuation
lessons.html: Quick check: Review the notes and complete the two exercises, then answer these to confirm you understood Punctuation.

questions.question: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
options: We bought apples oranges and pears.
We bought apples, oranges, and pears.

questions.explanation: Commas correctly separate items in a list.

questions.explanation: A singular possessive adds an apostrophe before the 's': 'dog's'.

options: I was tired; so I slept.
I was tired, I went to sleep;
I was tired; I went to sleep.
questions.explanation: A semicolon joins two closely related independent clauses without a conjunction.

lessons.title: 2.19 Common Grammar Errors
lessons.html:
📖 Common Grammar Errors
Know the usual traps and step around them.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Common Grammar Errors

Common Grammar Errors is the focus of this English Grammar Fundamentals lesson. It develops the learner's ability to construct accurate Standard English sentences.

grammar rule

A convention governing how words and clauses form sentences.

accuracy

Correct use of language forms and conventions.

sentence pattern

An organized grammatical arrangement of words and clauses.

Some grammar mistakes appear again and again in writing. They include confusing similar words, mismatching subjects and verbs, joining sentences wrongly, and misusing apostrophes. Learning to recognise these patterns helps you catch and fix them when you proofread.

Careful editing turns a good draft into a polished piece.

Key points

  • Their / there / they're – possession, place, and 'they are'.
  • Its / it's – 'its' shows possession; 'it's' means 'it is'.
  • Run-on and comma splice – do not join two sentences with only a comma.
  • Fewer / less and me / I – 'fewer' for countable, and use 'I' as a subject.

Example

Wrong: Its raining, so their going home, its too wet. Right: It's raining, so they're going home; it's too wet.

Why this matters

These small errors are highly visible and can lower your marks or your credibility at work. Learning the common traps and proofreading for them makes your academic and professional English clean, clear, and trustworthy.

📖 Everyday Vocabulary
The words that carry daily life.

Everyday Vocabulary

Everyday Vocabulary is the focus of this Vocabulary Development lesson. It develops the learner's ability to understand and use precise vocabulary confidently.

context

word form

Everyday vocabulary is the set of common words we use in ordinary situations, at home, in the market, on the road, and with friends. These words describe food, family, travel, work, weather, and daily routines.

Mastering everyday words first gives you a strong base before you add academic and professional terms.

Key points

  • High frequency – these words appear again and again, so they are worth learning first.
  • Practical – they help you handle real situations smoothly.
  • Foundational – they support understanding of harder texts later.

Example

Words such as market, price, change, bargain, bus, fare, neighbour, and rain are everyday vocabulary. In a sentence: I took the bus to the market and bargained for a fair price on rice.

Why this matters

Everyday vocabulary lets you communicate comfortably and builds the confidence you need for more formal English. Even in professional life, clear simple words often work best. A strong everyday base makes all later learning easier.

context

word form

Words that naturally and frequently occur together.

Academic vocabulary is the set of words used often in textbooks, essays, exams, and lectures across many subjects. Words like analyse, evidence, factor, and significant appear in science, history, and business alike.

These words help you explain ideas, compare information, and argue clearly.

Key points

  • Cross-subject – the same academic words appear in many courses.
  • Precise – they express exact meaning, useful for essays and exams.
  • Formal – they replace casual words with more scholarly ones.

Example

Instead of writing This shows the plan was good, an academic version reads: The results indicate that the strategy was effective. Words like indicate, results, strategy, and effective are academic vocabulary.

Why this matters

University study demands this vocabulary in every written and spoken task. Students who use academic words correctly write stronger essays and score higher marks. Building this word bank prepares you for higher education and any career that involves research or reports.

Professional vocabulary is the language used in the workplace to communicate clearly and politely. It includes words for tasks, meetings, deadlines, teamwork, and workplace roles.

Using the right professional words shows you are competent and easy to work with.

Key points

  • Action words – schedule, submit, follow up, complete.
  • Role words – supervisor, colleague, client, applicant.
  • Courtesy – professional language stays polite and respectful.

In an office message: I have submitted the report to my supervisor and will follow up with the client on Monday. Please let me know if you need any assistance. Words like submitted, supervisor, follow up, client, and assistance are professional vocabulary.

Why this matters

Employers judge you partly by how you communicate. The right professional vocabulary makes your emails, meetings, and interviews clear and confident. Whether you work in an NGO, a bank, or your own business, these words help you build trust and get results.

Business English terms are the specialized words used in trade, finance, management, and commerce. They cover money, contracts, marketing, and everyday business operations.

A business owner says: After paying our suppliers, our profit this month was small, so we must review the budget and negotiate better prices. Terms like suppliers, profit, budget, and negotiate are business English.

Why this matters

Business is central to life across West Africa, from market stalls to growing companies. Knowing these terms lets you write invoices, understand contracts, and speak with banks and partners. Strong business English can directly improve your income and opportunities.

lessons.title: 3.5 Word Formation
lessons.html:
📖 Word Formation
Grow one word into a family.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Word Formation

Word Formation is the focus of this Vocabulary Development lesson. It develops the learner's ability to understand and use precise vocabulary confidently.

context

The surrounding language and situation that help determine meaning.

word form

A grammatical version of a word, such as noun, verb, or adjective.

collocation

Words that naturally and frequently occur together.

Word formation is the process of building new words from a base word by changing its form. From one root, you can make nouns, verbs, adjectives, and adverbs, expanding your vocabulary quickly.

Understanding word families helps you recognise and use many words from a single root.

Key points

  • Root word – the base that carries the core meaning.
  • Adding parts – prefixes and suffixes change meaning or word class.
  • Word families – related words share the same root.

Example

From the root educate we form: educate (verb), education (noun), educator (noun), educational (adjective), educationally (adverb). In a sentence: The educator gave an educational talk that improved our education.

Why this matters

Learning one root can unlock five or more words, making your vocabulary grow fast. In essays and reports, knowing the correct form, such as choosing analysis or analyse, keeps your grammar accurate. Word formation is a powerful shortcut to advanced English.

lessons.title: 3.6 Prefixes & Suffixes
lessons.html:
📖 Prefixes and Suffixes
Small parts that change big meaning.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Prefixes & Suffixes

Prefixes & Suffixes is the focus of this Vocabulary Development lesson. It develops the learner's ability to understand and use precise vocabulary confidently.

context

The surrounding language and situation that help determine meaning.

word form

A grammatical version of a word, such as noun, verb, or adjective.

collocation

Words that naturally and frequently occur together.

A prefix is a group of letters added to the front of a word, and a suffix is added to the end. Both change a word's meaning or its part of speech. Learning common ones helps you understand new words without a dictionary.

Prefixes often change meaning; suffixes often change word class.

Key points

  • Prefix – added before, e.g. un-, re-, dis-, pre-, in-.
  • Suffix – added after, e.g. -tion, -ful, -ly, -ness, -able.
  • Meaning clues – un- means not, re- means again.

Example

Prefix: happy becomes unhappy (not happy); do becomes redo (do again). Suffix: care becomes careful (adjective) and carefully (adverb); happy becomes happiness (noun). Sentence: She carefully rewrote the unhappy ending.

Why this matters

Prefixes and suffixes let you guess the meaning of unfamiliar words, which is vital in exams and reading reports. They also help you form the correct word in writing. This knowledge multiplies your vocabulary and sharpens your accuracy in academic and professional English.

lessons.title: 3.7 Synonyms & Antonyms

📖 Synonyms and Antonyms
Say it differently, say it precisely.

Key Words & Meanings

Synonyms & Antonyms

Synonyms & Antonyms is the focus of this Vocabulary Development lesson. It develops the learner's ability to understand and use precise vocabulary confidently.

context

The surrounding language and situation that help determine meaning.

word form

A grammatical version of a word, such as noun, verb, or adjective.

collocation

Words that naturally and frequently occur together.

A synonym is a word with a similar meaning to another word, and an antonym is a word with the opposite meaning. Knowing both helps you vary your language and express exact shades of meaning.

Using synonyms avoids repetition, while antonyms help you show contrast clearly.

Key points

  • Synonym – similar meaning, e.g. big and large.
  • Antonym – opposite meaning, e.g. big and small.
  • Shades of meaning – synonyms are close but not always identical.

Example

Synonyms for happy: glad, pleased, joyful. Antonyms: sad, unhappy. Instead of repeating good, you might write: The plan was excellent, and the results were impressive. To show contrast: The first idea was strong, but the second was weak.

Why this matters

Rich vocabulary makes your writing and speech more interesting and precise. In essays, varied word choice earns higher marks; at work, it makes you sound confident and clear. Synonyms and antonyms give you the flexibility every skilled communicator needs.

lessons.title: 3.8 Collocations

📖 Collocations
Words that naturally go together.

Collocations

Collocations is the focus of this Vocabulary Development lesson. It develops the learner's ability to understand and use precise vocabulary confidently.

context

The surrounding language and situation that help determine meaning.

word form

A grammatical version of a word, such as noun, verb, or adjective.

collocation

Words that naturally and frequently occur together.

A collocation is a pair or group of words that native speakers regularly use together. We say make a mistake, not do a mistake, even though both seem logical. Learning collocations makes your English sound natural.

These natural word partnerships are learned by noticing patterns, not by rules alone.

Key points

  • Fixed pairs – certain words simply belong together.
  • Common verbs – make, do, take, have often form collocations.
  • Sound natural – correct collocations show fluency.

Example

Correct: make a decision, do homework, take a break, heavy rain, strong coffee. Incorrect: do a decision, make homework, strong rain. Sentence: We need to make an important decision before we take a break.

Why this matters

Using the right collocations is what separates natural, professional English from awkward English. In writing and speaking, correct word partners make you clear and credible. Noticing and collecting collocations as you read is one of the fastest ways to sound fluent.

lessons.title: 3.9 Idioms
lessons.html:
📖 Idioms
When words mean more than they say.

Idioms is the focus of this Vocabulary Development lesson. It develops the learner's ability to understand and use precise vocabulary confidently.

context

The surrounding language and situation that help determine meaning.

word form

A grammatical version of a word, such as noun, verb, or adjective.

collocation

Words that naturally and frequently occur together.

An idiom is a common expression whose meaning is different from the literal meaning of its words. When someone says it is raining cats and dogs, no animals are falling; it simply means it is raining heavily.

Idioms add colour to English, but they must be learned as whole phrases.

Key points

  • Figurative meaning – the real meaning is not literal.
  • Fixed form – the words usually cannot be changed.
  • Context matters – idioms suit informal or friendly settings more than formal reports.

Example

Break the ice means to start a conversation and make people comfortable. A piece of cake means very easy. Sentence: The interview felt like a piece of cake once the manager broke the ice with a friendly joke.

Why this matters

Idioms appear often in conversation, films, and news, so understanding them helps you follow real English. Using a few well helps you connect with others. However, in formal academic writing, use idioms carefully, choosing plain language when precision matters most.

lessons.title: 3.10 Phrasal Verbs
lessons.html:
📖 Phrasal Verbs
A verb plus a small word, a whole new meaning.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Phrasal Verbs

Phrasal Verbs is the focus of this Vocabulary Development lesson. It develops the learner's ability to understand and use precise vocabulary confidently.

context

The surrounding language and situation that help determine meaning.

word form

A grammatical version of a word, such as noun, verb, or adjective.

collocation

Words that naturally and frequently occur together.

A phrasal verb is a verb combined with a preposition or adverb that together create a new meaning. For example, give up does not mean to give; it means to stop trying. English uses phrasal verbs constantly.

The small word can change the meaning completely, so learn them as units.

Key points

  • Verb plus particle – e.g. look after, turn on, find out.
  • New meaning – the whole phrase means something different from the verb alone.
  • Very common – used more in speech and informal writing.

Example

Turn on means to start a machine; look after means to care for; find out means to discover. Sentence: Please turn on the generator and look after the office while I find out why the power went off.

Why this matters

Phrasal verbs are everywhere in everyday and workplace English, so understanding them is essential for real communication. Using them correctly makes your speech sound natural. In formal writing, you can often choose a single-word alternative such as discover instead of find out.

lessons.title: 3.11 Context Clues
lessons.html:
📖 Context Clues
Let the sentence teach you the word.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Context Clues

Context Clues is the focus of this Vocabulary Development lesson. It develops the learner's ability to understand and use precise vocabulary confidently.

context

The surrounding language and situation that help determine meaning.

word form

A grammatical version of a word, such as noun, verb, or adjective.

collocation

Words that naturally and frequently occur together.

Context clues are hints within a sentence or paragraph that help you guess the meaning of an unfamiliar word. Instead of stopping to check every new word, you use the surrounding words to work out the meaning.

This skill keeps your reading smooth and builds independence.

Key points

  • Definition clue – the meaning is explained nearby.
  • Example clue – examples show what the word means.
  • Contrast clue – words like but or unlike show the opposite meaning.

Example

Read: The farmer was elated, or extremely happy, when the rains finally came. The phrase or extremely happy is a definition clue telling you that elated means very happy, even if you never saw the word before.

Why this matters

In exams and at work, you cannot always reach for a dictionary. Context clues let you keep reading confidently and understand new material quickly. This skill is essential for handling textbooks, reports, and articles, and it steadily grows your vocabulary through reading.

lessons.title: 3.12 Vocabulary Building Strategies
lessons.html:
📖 Vocabulary Building Strategies
Grow your word bank on purpose.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Vocabulary Building Strategies

Vocabulary Building Strategies is the focus of this Vocabulary Development lesson. It develops the learner's ability to understand and use precise vocabulary confidently.

context

The surrounding language and situation that help determine meaning.

word form

A grammatical version of a word, such as noun, verb, or adjective.

collocation

Words that naturally and frequently occur together.

Vocabulary building strategies are the practical methods you use to learn and remember new words steadily. A rich vocabulary is built not by chance but by consistent, active habits.

The best strategies help you not only meet new words but truly own them.

Steps

  1. Keep a word notebook and write each new word with its meaning and an example sentence.
  2. Learn words in context, not as lonely lists, so you remember how to use them.
  3. Use spaced repetition, reviewing words after one day, one week, and one month.
  4. Group by topic or word family to make connections stronger.
  5. Use new words quickly in speaking and writing to lock them in.

Example

A learner meets the word negotiate in a news article. She writes: negotiate - to discuss to reach an agreement. Example: We will negotiate the price with the supplier. She reviews it during the week and uses it in her own market talk.

Why this matters

A strong vocabulary is the heart of good reading, writing, speaking, and listening. Using deliberate strategies means your word bank grows every week, helping you excel in exams, interviews, and any professional setting.

lessons.title: 4.1 Reading Strategies
lessons.html:
📖 Reading Strategies
Good readers do not read every word the same way.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Reading Strategies

Reading Strategies is the focus of this Reading Skills lesson. It develops the learner's ability to understand texts and support interpretations with evidence.

main idea

The central point that unifies a text.

supporting evidence

Information that proves or develops an idea.

inference

A logical conclusion based on textual clues.

Reading strategies are the smart habits you use before, during, and after reading so that you understand and remember more. Instead of reading everything slowly from start to finish, skilled readers adjust their approach to fit their purpose.

Think of it like travelling in Monrovia: sometimes you walk slowly to see everything, and sometimes you take a quick taxi straight to your destination. Reading works the same way.

Steps

  1. Before reading, ask yourself why you are reading and what you already know.
  2. Preview the title, headings, and pictures to predict the content.
  3. While reading, ask questions and connect ideas to your own life.
  4. Underline key points or write short notes in the margin.
  5. After reading, summarise the main idea in one or two sentences.

Example

Before reading an article titled Farming in Bong County, you predict it will discuss crops and rainfall. You then read to confirm, underlining facts about rice production.

Why this matters

In school and at work, you will face long reports, textbooks, and emails. Strong strategies help you find what you need quickly, understand deeply, and avoid wasting time.

lessons.title: 4.2 Skimming
lessons.html:
📖 Skimming
Read fast to catch the big picture.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Skimming

Skimming is the focus of this Reading Skills lesson. It develops the learner's ability to understand texts and support interpretations with evidence.

main idea

The central point that unifies a text.

supporting evidence

Information that proves or develops an idea.

inference

A logical conclusion based on textual clues.

Skimming means reading a text quickly to get the general idea without reading every word. Your eyes glide over the page, catching key words, headings, and the first sentences of paragraphs.

Skimming answers the question, What is this text about? It does not give you every detail, but it gives you the overall meaning fast.

Steps

  1. Read the title, subtitles, and any bold or highlighted words.
  2. Read the first and last paragraphs fully.
  3. Read only the first sentence of each middle paragraph.
  4. Let your eyes move quickly, ignoring small words.
  5. In your mind, sum up the main topic in one line.

Example

You receive a three page newsletter from your church. In thirty seconds you skim the headings and learn it covers a fundraising drive, a youth meeting, and a thank you note, so you know where to focus.

Why this matters

Students and professionals face far more reading than time allows. Skimming lets you decide quickly whether a document is worth reading closely, so you save time for what truly matters.

lessons.title: 4.3 Scanning
lessons.html:
📖 Scanning
Hunt the page for one exact piece of information.

Key Words & Meanings

Scanning

Scanning is the focus of this Reading Skills lesson. It develops the learner's ability to understand texts and support interpretations with evidence.

main idea

The central point that unifies a text.

supporting evidence

Information that proves or develops an idea.

inference

A logical conclusion based on textual clues.

Scanning means searching a text quickly to find a specific fact, such as a name, date, number, or word. Unlike skimming, you are not trying to understand the whole text. You are looking for one target.

Your eyes move fast down or across the page, ignoring everything except the thing you need.

Steps

  1. Decide exactly what you are looking for, such as a price or a name.
  2. Keep that key word clearly in your mind.
  3. Move your eyes quickly over the text, not reading full sentences.
  4. Watch for clues like capital letters, numbers, or symbols.
  5. Stop and read closely only when you find the target.

Example

You want to know when a bus leaves Ganta for Monrovia. You scan the timetable, skipping all other routes, until your eyes land on Ganta and the time 7:30 a.m.

Why this matters

At work you often need one figure from a long report, or one clause from a contract. Scanning finds it in seconds instead of forcing you to read the whole document.

lessons.title: 4.4 Identifying Main Ideas
lessons.html:
📖 Identifying Main Ideas
Every paragraph has one big point at its heart.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Identifying Main Ideas

Identifying Main Ideas is the focus of this Reading Skills lesson. It develops the learner's ability to understand texts and support interpretations with evidence.

main idea

The central point that unifies a text.

supporting evidence

Information that proves or develops an idea.

inference

A logical conclusion based on textual clues.

The main idea is the most important point the writer wants you to understand. It is the message the whole paragraph or text is built around. All the other sentences support, explain, or prove this main idea.

Often the main idea sits in the first or last sentence, but sometimes you must work it out yourself from the details.

Steps

  1. Read the whole paragraph once for a general sense.
  2. Ask yourself, What is this mostly about?
  3. Look at the first and last sentences, where main ideas often hide.
  4. Check whether the other sentences support this point.
  5. State the main idea in your own short sentence.

Example

A paragraph describes cassava, plantain, and rice grown near Kakata. The main idea is that the region produces many food crops. The individual crops are the supporting details.

Why this matters

Finding the main idea lets you summarise reports, answer exam questions, and follow a manager's instructions accurately. It is the foundation of clear understanding.

lessons.html: Quick check: Review the notes and complete the two exercises, then answer these to confirm you understood Identifying Main Ideas.

options: The central point the author wants to convey
The first word of the paragraph

questions.question: Where is the main idea of a paragraph most often stated?
options: Frequently in a topic sentence, often at the beginning

lessons.title: 4.5 Supporting Details
lessons.html:
📖 Supporting Details
Details are the proof behind the point.

Key Words & Meanings

Supporting Details

Supporting Details is the focus of this Reading Skills lesson. It develops the learner's ability to understand texts and support interpretations with evidence.

main idea

The central point that unifies a text.

supporting evidence

Information that proves or develops an idea.

inference

A logical conclusion based on textual clues.

Supporting details are the facts, examples, reasons, and descriptions that explain and strengthen the main idea. If the main idea is the trunk of a tree, the supporting details are the branches that hold it up.

Common types of details include examples, statistics, dates, reasons, and small descriptions.

Steps

  1. First identify the main idea of the paragraph.
  2. Ask, What facts or examples explain this point?
  3. Look for signal words like for example, because, and such as.
  4. Note numbers, names, and specific descriptions.
  5. Check how each detail connects back to the main idea.

Example

Main idea: The market at Red Light is busy. Supporting details: over a thousand traders sell there daily, buses arrive every few minutes, and vendors call out prices from morning until night.

Why this matters

In academic writing, details prove your argument. At work, details back up your recommendations. Recognising them helps you judge whether a claim is well supported or just an opinion.

lessons.title: 4.6 Making Inferences
lessons.html:
📖 Making Inferences
Read between the lines to find hidden meaning.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Making Inferences

Making Inferences is the focus of this Reading Skills lesson. It develops the learner's ability to understand texts and support interpretations with evidence.

main idea

The central point that unifies a text.

supporting evidence

Information that proves or develops an idea.

inference

A logical conclusion based on textual clues.

Making an inference means using clues in the text plus your own knowledge to understand something the writer did not state directly. Writers often suggest ideas rather than spell them out, and a good reader fills the gap.

An inference is a smart guess based on evidence, not a wild guess. The clues must point clearly to your conclusion.

Steps

  1. Read carefully and notice the details the writer gives.
  2. Ask, What is the writer hinting at but not saying?
  3. Combine the clues with what you already know.
  4. Form a reasonable conclusion.
  5. Check that the text supports your inference.

Example

A text says, Musu grabbed her umbrella and shut the windows before leaving. You infer that rain is coming, even though the writer never says the word rain.

Why this matters

Reports, contracts, and even emails often imply things politely instead of stating them. Making inferences helps you grasp true meaning, tone, and intention in academic and workplace communication.

options: It is based on textual evidence and reasonable logic
