questions.explanation: A valid inference is supported by evidence in the text combined with sound reasoning.

lessons.title: 4.7 Vocabulary in Context
lessons.html:
📖 Vocabulary in Context
The words around a new word reveal its meaning.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Vocabulary in Context

Vocabulary in Context is the focus of this Reading Skills lesson. It develops the learner's ability to understand texts and support interpretations with evidence.

main idea

The central point that unifies a text.

supporting evidence

Information that proves or develops an idea.

inference

A logical conclusion based on textual clues.

Vocabulary in context means working out what an unfamiliar word means by studying the sentence and paragraph around it. Instead of stopping to reach for a dictionary every time, you use nearby clues to guess the meaning.

Context clues include definitions, examples, contrasts, and the general sense of the passage.

Steps

  1. Read the full sentence containing the unknown word.
  2. Look for clues such as a definition or an example nearby.
  3. Notice contrast words like but or however that hint at opposites.
  4. Guess a meaning and replace the word with it to test the sense.
  5. Confirm later with a dictionary if the word is important.

Example

The road was impassable; heavy rains had washed it away completely. From the clue about washed away, you guess impassable means impossible to travel on.

Why this matters

In exams and at work you cannot always check a dictionary. Using context keeps you reading smoothly and builds your vocabulary naturally over time.

lessons.title: 4.8 Reading Academic Articles
lessons.html:
📖 Reading Academic Articles
Scholarly texts follow a pattern you can learn.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Reading Academic Articles

Reading Academic Articles is the focus of this Reading Skills lesson. It develops the learner's ability to understand texts and support interpretations with evidence.

main idea

The central point that unifies a text.

supporting evidence

Information that proves or develops an idea.

inference

A logical conclusion based on textual clues.

Academic articles are formal texts written by researchers to share findings. They use specialised vocabulary and follow a predictable structure, usually including an abstract, introduction, methods, results, and conclusion.

You do not have to read them from top to bottom. Reading strategically saves time and improves understanding.

Steps

  1. Read the abstract first to learn the main findings.
  2. Read the introduction to understand the research question.
  3. Skim the methods to see how the study was done.
  4. Focus on the results and conclusion for the key outcomes.
  5. Note unfamiliar terms and check them as you go.

Example

A University of Liberia student reads an article on malaria prevention. She reads the abstract, learns bed nets reduced cases by forty percent, and jumps straight to the results to confirm the figure.

Why this matters

Higher education and professional research depend on reading such articles. Knowing their structure lets you extract knowledge efficiently and cite reliable evidence in your own work.

lessons.title: 4.9 Reading Business Documents

📖 Reading Business Documents

A logical conclusion based on textual clues.

Business documents include emails, memos, reports, proposals, invoices, and contracts. They are usually written to inform, request, or persuade, and they value clarity and brevity. Reading them well means finding the purpose and action quickly.

Most business writing is organised so the most important information comes first.

Steps

  1. Check the subject line or title to learn the topic.
  2. Identify who wrote it and who it is meant for.
  3. Look for the main request or decision, often near the top.
  4. Scan for dates, amounts, and deadlines.
  5. Note any action you are expected to take.

Example

A memo at a Monrovia company reads, All staff must submit leave requests by 20 August. You quickly note the action and the deadline, then reply to confirm.

Why this matters

In any job you will handle documents daily. Reading them accurately prevents missed deadlines, costly errors, and misunderstandings with colleagues and clients.

lessons.title: 5.1 Active Listening
lessons.html:
📖 Active Listening
Hearing is easy; truly listening takes effort.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Active Listening

Active Listening is the focus of this Listening Skills lesson. It develops the learner's ability to understand spoken English, organize notes, and identify speaker meaning.

active listening

Focused listening for purpose, structure, and evidence.

signal phrase

Language marking an important relationship or change.

speaker intention

The purpose a speaker aims to achieve.

Active listening means paying full attention to a speaker, understanding their message, and showing that you are engaged. It is more than staying silent; it involves focus, thinking, and responding.

An active listener concentrates on meaning, not just words, and holds back distractions and early judgments.

Steps

  1. Face the speaker and give your full attention.
  2. Put away your phone and quiet your thoughts.
  3. Listen for the main message, not just individual words.
  4. Nod or use short words like I see to show you follow.
  5. Ask questions or repeat key points to confirm understanding.

Example

During a community meeting in Buchanan, you face the chief, keep eye contact, and afterwards say, So you are asking each household to contribute, which confirms you understood correctly.

Why this matters

Active listening builds trust, reduces mistakes, and helps you learn. In classrooms and workplaces, people value colleagues who listen carefully and respond thoughtfully.

lessons.html: Quick check: Review the notes and complete the two exercises, then answer these to confirm you understood Active Listening.

questions.question: Which behavior demonstrates active listening?

questions.explanation: Paraphrasing to confirm understanding is a core active listening technique.

It proves you disagree with the speaker
It replaces the need to understand the words

lessons.title: 5.2 Listening for Main Ideas
lessons.html:
📖 Listening for Main Ideas
Catch the big message, not every single word.

Key Words & Meanings

Listening for Main Ideas

Listening for Main Ideas is the focus of this Listening Skills lesson. It develops the learner's ability to understand spoken English, organize notes, and identify speaker meaning.

active listening

Focused listening for purpose, structure, and evidence.

signal phrase

Language marking an important relationship or change.

speaker intention

The purpose a speaker aims to achieve.

Listening for main ideas means focusing on the speaker's most important point rather than trying to remember every detail. Just as texts have main ideas, so do speeches, lectures, and conversations.

Speakers often signal their main points with phrases like the most important thing or in summary.

Steps

  1. Relax and focus on the overall message.
  2. Listen for signal phrases such as my main point is.
  3. Notice ideas the speaker repeats or emphasises.
  4. Pay attention to the opening and closing, where main ideas appear.
  5. Sum up the message in one short sentence in your mind.

Example

A health worker speaks for ten minutes about clean water. You catch the main idea: boiling water before drinking prevents disease, even if you miss some smaller details.

Why this matters

In lectures and meetings, you cannot record everything. Grasping the main idea keeps you oriented and helps you follow the discussion even when details rush past.

lessons.html: Quick check: Review the notes and complete the two exercises, then answer these to confirm you understood Listening for Main Ideas.

questions.question: When listening for the main idea, what should you focus on?

Only the first word of each sentence
questions.explanation: Listening for the main idea means grasping the speaker's overall central point.

lessons.title: 5.3 Listening for Details
lessons.html:
📖 Listening for Details
Sometimes the small facts matter most.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Listening for Details

Listening for Details is the focus of this Listening Skills lesson. It develops the learner's ability to understand spoken English, organize notes, and identify speaker meaning.

active listening

Focused listening for purpose, structure, and evidence.

signal phrase

Language marking an important relationship or change.

speaker intention

The purpose a speaker aims to achieve.

Listening for details means concentrating on specific pieces of information such as names, numbers, dates, times, and instructions. Once you know the main idea, details fill in the exact facts you may need to act on.

This kind of listening requires sharp focus, because a single missed number can change everything.

Steps

  1. Know in advance what details you must catch.
  2. Listen for numbers, names, places, and times.
  3. Notice ordering words like first, next, and finally.
  4. Jot down key facts as you hear them.
  5. Repeat details back to confirm you heard correctly.

Example

Your supervisor says, Deliver the goods to Sinkor by 3 p.m. on Friday. You catch the place, the time, and the day, then write them down at once.

Why this matters

Following instructions, taking phone messages, and recording data all depend on catching details. Accuracy here protects you from costly mistakes at work and in study.

options: Deciding the general mood of a song

lessons.title: 5.4 Note-Taking Skills
lessons.html:
📖 Note-Taking Skills
Good notes turn spoken words into lasting knowledge.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Note-Taking Skills

Note-Taking Skills is the focus of this Listening Skills lesson. It develops the learner's ability to understand spoken English, organize notes, and identify speaker meaning.

active listening

Focused listening for purpose, structure, and evidence.

signal phrase

Language marking an important relationship or change.

speaker intention

The purpose a speaker aims to achieve.

Note-taking is the skill of writing down key information while listening or reading, so you can remember and review it later. Good notes are short, organised, and in your own words, not a full copy of everything said.

You cannot write every word, so you must select what matters most.

Steps

  1. Write the topic and date at the top.
  2. Record only main ideas and key details, not every word.
  3. Use short forms, symbols, and abbreviations to keep up.
  4. Organise with headings, bullets, and spacing.
  5. Review and tidy your notes soon after, while memory is fresh.

Example

In a training session you write: Water safety - boil 1 min - store covered - clean cup. These few words capture a long explanation clearly.

Why this matters

Students revise from notes before exams, and workers rely on notes from meetings to complete tasks. Strong note-taking saves your memory and keeps you accountable.

lessons.title: 5.5 Listening to Lectures
lessons.html:
📖 Listening to Lectures
A lecture is a river of ideas; learn to swim with it.

Key Words & Meanings

Listening to Lectures is the focus of this Listening Skills lesson. It develops the learner's ability to understand spoken English, organize notes, and identify speaker meaning.

Focused listening for purpose, structure, and evidence.

signal phrase

speaker intention

Listening to lectures is a special skill because lectures are long, formal, and full of information. The speaker usually follows a clear plan, moving from an introduction through main points to a conclusion.

Success depends on staying focused, following the structure, and taking useful notes at the same time.

Steps

  1. Prepare by reviewing the topic before the lecture.
  2. Listen for the outline the lecturer gives at the start.
  3. Track signal words like firstly, moreover, and therefore.
  4. Note main points and examples, leaving space to add more.
  5. Review your notes afterwards and fill any gaps.

Example

At a University of Liberia economics lecture, you hear the lecturer say, Today we cover three causes of inflation. You number your page one to three and fill each as she speaks.

Why this matters

Higher education relies heavily on lectures. Mastering this skill lets you absorb knowledge, prepare for exams, and keep pace with fast, information rich teaching.

lessons.title: 5.6 Listening to Business Meetings

📖 Listening to Business Meetings
Meetings decide what happens next at work.

Tap a word to open its definition.

Listening to Business Meetings

Listening to Business Meetings is the focus of this Listening Skills lesson. It develops the learner's ability to understand spoken English, organize notes, and identify speaker meaning.

Listening in business meetings means following discussions, tracking decisions, and noting the tasks assigned to you and others. Meetings often move quickly, with several people speaking, so focused listening is essential.

Key things to catch are decisions, action items, deadlines, and who is responsible for each task.

Steps

  1. Read the agenda beforehand so you know the topics.
  2. Identify who is speaking and their role.
  3. Listen for decisions and the reasons behind them.
  4. Note action items, deadlines, and names of responsible people.
  5. Ask for clarification if a point or task is unclear.

Example

In a staff meeting, the manager says, Fatu will prepare the budget by Monday. You note: Fatu, budget, Monday, so the task and deadline are clear.

Why this matters

Missing a decision or a deadline in a meeting can hurt your reputation and the whole team. Careful listening keeps you informed, reliable, and ready to act.

lessons.title: 5.7 Understanding Different English Accents
lessons.html:
📖 Understanding Different English Accents
English sounds different across the world, yet the words are the same.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Understanding Different English Accents

Understanding Different English Accents is the focus of this Listening Skills lesson. It develops the learner's ability to understand spoken English, organize notes, and identify speaker meaning.

active listening

Focused listening for purpose, structure, and evidence.

signal phrase

Language marking an important relationship or change.

speaker intention

The purpose a speaker aims to achieve.

English is spoken with many accents, from Liberian and Nigerian English to British, American, Indian, and more. An accent is simply the way sounds, rhythm, and stress differ from region to region. The vocabulary and grammar remain largely the same.

With practice, your ear adjusts and understanding becomes easier.

Steps

  1. Focus on the whole message rather than every single sound.
  2. Use context and body language to fill any gaps.
  3. Expose your ear to varied accents through radio, film, and podcasts.
  4. Politely ask the speaker to repeat or slow down when needed.
  5. Note common sound differences so they surprise you less next time.

Example

On a call with a British client, the word schedule sounds unfamiliar, but from the context of dates and times you understand she means the timetable.

Why this matters

Academic and professional life is global. You will study with, work for, and serve people from many nations. Understanding diverse accents makes you a confident, effective communicator anywhere.

lessons.title: 6.1 Pronunciation
lessons.html:
📖 Pronunciation
The way you say a word can help or hide your meaning.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Pronunciation

Pronunciation is the focus of this Speaking Skills lesson. It develops the learner's ability to communicate ideas clearly, fluently, and appropriately.

fluency

The ability to speak smoothly at an understandable pace.

pronunciation

The clear production of speech sounds.

audience awareness

Adaptation of language and delivery to listeners.

Pronunciation is how we produce the sounds of English so that listeners understand us clearly. It covers individual sounds (like the difference between ship and sheep), word stress (SEV-en, not sev-EN), and clear endings such as the final -s and -ed.

You do not need a foreign accent to be understood. The goal is clarity, not imitation. Even with your natural Liberian voice, careful sounds make your message land.

Steps

  1. Listen to a word first, then repeat it slowly.
  2. Break long words into syllables: o-ppor-tu-ni-ty.
  3. Find the stressed syllable and say it a little louder and longer.
  4. Practise tricky sounds like /th/ in think and this.
  5. Record yourself and compare with a clear model.

Example

Say aloud: I would like to REG-is-ter for the a-CA-de-mic PRO-gramme. Stress the capital syllables and finish each word fully.

Why this matters

In interviews, presentations, and phone calls, clear pronunciation builds trust. When employers and lecturers understand you the first time, you sound confident and professional.

lessons.html: Quick check: Review the notes and complete the two exercises, then answer these to confirm you understood Pronunciation.

questions.question: Which pair of words are minimal pairs that a learner might confuse because they differ by a single sound?

questions.question: What does word stress mean when pronouncing a multi-syllable word like PHOtograph?
options: Making one syllable louder, longer, and clearer than the others
Saying every syllable at the same volume
questions.explanation: Word stress means giving one syllable more emphasis in loudness, length, and clarity than the rest.

questions.question: Why can the letter combination -ough be difficult for learners of English pronunciation?
options: It can be pronounced several different ways in different words
It is only used in formal writing
It is never found at the end of a word
questions.explanation: The spelling -ough maps to several different sounds, as in through, tough, and though, so spelling does not predict pronunciation.

lessons.title: 6.2 Intonation
lessons.html:
📖 Intonation
Your voice sings a tune that carries meaning.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Intonation

Intonation is the focus of this Speaking Skills lesson. It develops the learner's ability to communicate ideas clearly, fluently, and appropriately.

fluency

The ability to speak smoothly at an understandable pace.

pronunciation

The clear production of speech sounds.

audience awareness

Adaptation of language and delivery to listeners.

Intonation is the rise and fall of your voice as you speak. It shows whether you are asking, telling, listing, or feeling surprised. The same words can sound polite or rude depending on the tune you give them.

English usually rises at the end of yes/no questions and falls at the end of statements. Listing items goes up, up, up, then falls on the last one.

Steps

  1. Decide your purpose: statement, question, or list.
  2. Let your voice fall at the end of a normal statement.
  3. Let your voice rise at the end of a yes/no question.
  4. Stress the most important word in the sentence.
  5. Read the sentence aloud twice, exaggerating the tune.

Example

Statement (falling): The meeting is on Monday.↓ Question (rising): Is the meeting on Monday?↑ List: We need pens,↑ paper,↑ and a laptop.↓

Why this matters

Good intonation keeps listeners interested and shows respect. In a business meeting or classroom debate, the right tune makes you sound warm, sure, and easy to follow instead of flat or harsh.

questions.question: What does a speaker usually communicate by using a falling intonation at the end of a statement?

lessons.title: 6.3 Fluency Development
lessons.html:
📖 Fluency Development
Speaking smoothly matters more than speaking fast.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Fluency Development

Fluency Development is the focus of this Speaking Skills lesson. It develops the learner's ability to communicate ideas clearly, fluently, and appropriately.

fluency

The ability to speak smoothly at an understandable pace.

pronunciation

The clear production of speech sounds.

audience awareness

Adaptation of language and delivery to listeners.

Fluency is the ability to speak in a smooth, connected flow without too many long pauses or false starts. A fluent speaker keeps ideas moving, links words naturally, and recovers quickly when they lose their way.

Fluency grows through use, not memorising rules. The more you speak, the more automatic the words become.

Steps

  1. Speak in short, complete phrases rather than single words.
  2. Use fillers wisely: well, let me think, in fact.
  3. If you forget a word, describe it instead of stopping.
  4. Practise talking for one minute on a familiar topic daily.
  5. Read aloud each day to train your mouth and breath.

Example

Instead of stopping when you forget generator, keep going: Well, we use the machine that gives us light when NEPA is off.

Why this matters

In job interviews and group projects, fluent speech shows you can think and communicate under pressure. Smooth speaking helps people follow your ideas and see you as capable and confident.

questions.question: Why is regular speaking practice important for developing fluency?
options: It guarantees a perfect native accent
It removes the need to learn grammar
It builds automaticity so words come more quickly and naturally
questions.explanation: Frequent practice builds automaticity, letting the speaker produce language faster and with less hesitation.

lessons.title: 6.4 Everyday Conversations
lessons.html:
📖 Everyday Conversations
Small talk opens big doors.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Everyday Conversations

Everyday Conversations is the focus of this Speaking Skills lesson. It develops the learner's ability to communicate ideas clearly, fluently, and appropriately.

fluency

The ability to speak smoothly at an understandable pace.

pronunciation

The clear production of speech sounds.

audience awareness

Adaptation of language and delivery to listeners.

Everyday conversations are the ordinary exchanges we have with neighbours, classmates, customers, and colleagues. They include greetings, small talk, asking for directions, shopping, and sharing news. Doing them well makes daily life and work easier.

Good conversation is a two-way road: you speak, you listen, and you respond to what the other person actually says.

Steps

  1. Open with a friendly greeting and a smile.
  2. Ask a simple question to show interest.
  3. Listen fully before you reply.
  4. Take turns; do not talk over the other person.
  5. Close politely: It was nice talking with you.

Example

At the market: Good morning, ma. How is the day going? Please, how much for the rice? Thank you, I will take two cups.

Why this matters

Everyday conversation skills build relationships that lead to jobs, customers, and friendships. At work, easy small talk with colleagues creates a warm team and shows you are approachable and professional.

lessons.title: 6.5 Academic Discussions
lessons.html:
📖 Academic Discussions
In class, sharing ideas well is a skill you can learn.

Key Words & Meanings

Academic Discussions

Academic Discussions is the focus of this Speaking Skills lesson. It develops the learner's ability to communicate ideas clearly, fluently, and appropriately.

fluency

The ability to speak smoothly at an understandable pace.

pronunciation

The clear production of speech sounds.

audience awareness

Adaptation of language and delivery to listeners.

Academic discussions are focused talks in classrooms, seminars, and study groups where learners share ideas, ask questions, and challenge points respectfully. The goal is to build knowledge together, not to win an argument.

Strong contributors give reasons and evidence, and they connect their ideas to what others have said.

Steps

  1. Prepare by reading and noting your main points.
  2. State your idea clearly, then support it with a reason.
  3. Use polite phrases to agree or disagree.
  4. Refer to others: Building on what Musu said...
  5. Ask questions when you need clarity.

Example

Say: I see your point, but I think farming can grow the economy because it creates many jobs in rural counties.

Why this matters

University lecturers and employers value people who can discuss ideas with reason and respect. These skills help you contribute in tutorials, defend a project, and take part in team decisions at work.

📖 Public Speaking

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Public Speaking

fluency

audience awareness

Public speaking is delivering a message to an audience, such as a speech at a ceremony, a talk at church, or a report to a community meeting. It combines a clear message, a confident voice, and good body language.

Nervousness is normal. Preparation and practice turn fear into energy.

Steps

  1. Know your audience and your main message.
  2. Plan an opening, three key points, and a closing.
  3. Practise aloud several times, ideally standing up.
  4. Make eye contact and stand tall.
  5. Breathe slowly and pause between ideas.

Example

Opening line: Good afternoon, everyone. Today I want to share three simple ways our community in Monrovia can keep our streets clean.

Why this matters

Public speaking helps you lead, persuade, and represent your organisation. Whether you pitch a business idea or address a graduation, a confident speaker earns respect and moves people to act.

lessons.title: 6.7 Business Meetings

📖 Business Meetings
Meetings run on clear speaking and good listening.

Key Words & Meanings

Business Meetings

Business Meetings is the focus of this Speaking Skills lesson. It develops the learner's ability to communicate ideas clearly, fluently, and appropriately.

fluency

The ability to speak smoothly at an understandable pace.

pronunciation

The clear production of speech sounds.

audience awareness

Adaptation of language and delivery to listeners.

Business meetings are organised gatherings where colleagues plan, decide, and report on work. Speaking well in a meeting means sharing your point clearly, respecting the agenda, and helping the group reach decisions.

Every meeting has a purpose. Knowing that purpose helps you contribute at the right time.

Steps

  1. Read the agenda and prepare your points before you arrive.
  2. Wait for the right moment, then speak clearly and briefly.
  3. Use polite openers: May I add something?
  4. Support ideas with facts, not just opinions.
  5. Note action points and who is responsible.

Example

Say: Thank you, Chair. I suggest we open the shop by 8 a.m. because most customers pass here early on their way to work.

Why this matters

Meetings are where careers are noticed. Speaking clearly and respectfully shows managers you are organised and reliable, and it helps your team make faster, better decisions.

📖 Telephone Communication
On the phone, your voice is your whole face.

Key Words & Meanings

Telephone Communication

fluency

pronunciation

audience awareness

Adaptation of language and delivery to listeners.

Telephone communication is speaking clearly and politely when the listener cannot see you. Because there are no gestures or facial expressions, your words, tone, and clarity carry everything.

A professional call has a clear opening, a clear purpose, and a clear closing.

Steps

  1. Greet and identify yourself and your organisation.
  2. State the reason for your call in one sentence.
  3. Speak slowly and confirm names and numbers.
  4. Take notes on key points and next steps.
  5. Thank the person and close politely.

Example

Say: Good morning, this is James from Tolbert Innovation Hub. I am calling to confirm your class for Monday. May I have your full name, please?

Why this matters

Many jobs handle customers and partners by phone. A clear, polite phone manner protects your organisation's reputation and helps you book clients, solve problems, and sound professional from the first hello.

lessons.title: 6.9 Presentation Skills

📖 Presentation Skills
A good presentation guides the audience step by step.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Presentation Skills

Presentation Skills is the focus of this Speaking Skills lesson. It develops the learner's ability to communicate ideas clearly, fluently, and appropriately.

fluency

The ability to speak smoothly at an understandable pace.

pronunciation

The clear production of speech sounds.

audience awareness

Adaptation of language and delivery to listeners.

Presentation skills are the abilities you use to share information in an organised, engaging way, often with slides or visual aids. A strong presentation has a clear structure, simple visuals, and a confident delivery.

The best presenters keep it simple: one main idea per slide and plenty of eye contact with the room.

Steps

  1. Start with a clear title and your main goal.
  2. Organise content into a beginning, middle, and end.
  3. Use few words on slides; talk to explain them.
  4. Practise timing so you do not rush or run over.
  5. End with a summary and a call to action.

Example

Closing slide line: To sum up, our tailoring group can grow if we train more youth, buy two new machines, and advertise on the radio.

Why this matters

Presentations sell ideas, projects, and proposals. Students present research and workers pitch plans to bosses and donors. Doing it well helps you win support, funding, and recognition.

lessons.title: 7.1 Sentence Writing
lessons.html:
📖 Sentence Writing
Every strong paragraph begins with a strong sentence.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Sentence Writing

Sentence Writing is the focus of this Writing Fundamentals lesson. It develops the learner's ability to write clear, organized, and accurate texts.

coherence

The clear and logical progression of ideas.

revision

Improvement of meaning, structure, and language after drafting.

proofreading

A final check for grammar, spelling, and punctuation.

A sentence is a group of words that expresses a complete thought. It needs a subject (who or what) and a verb (the action or state), and it begins with a capital letter and ends with a full stop, question mark, or exclamation mark.

Good sentences are complete and clear. Avoid fragments (incomplete thoughts) and run-ons (two sentences joined without proper punctuation).

Steps

  1. Choose a subject: who or what the sentence is about.
  2. Add a verb that tells what the subject does or is.
  3. Add details to make the meaning clear.
  4. Start with a capital letter and end with the right mark.
  5. Read it aloud to check it makes complete sense.

Example

Model sentence: The students at the hub practise English every evening. Subject: the students; verb: practise; details: English every evening.

Why this matters

Sentences are the building blocks of every report, email, and exam answer. Writing complete, correct sentences makes you look educated and careful, and it keeps your reader from getting confused.

lessons.title: 📝 Practice: Sentence Writing
lessons.html: Quick check: Review the notes and complete the two exercises, then answer these to confirm you understood Sentence Writing.

options: A comma splice joining two independent clauses
questions.explanation: Two independent clauses joined only by a comma form a comma splice, which needs a conjunction or semicolon.

options: She studied hard, and she passed the exam.
She studied hard she passed the exam.
She studied hard, she passed the exam.
She studied hard although passed the exam.
questions.explanation: Two independent clauses joined by a comma and the coordinating conjunction and form a correct compound sentence.

lessons.title: 7.2 Paragraph Writing
lessons.html:
📖 Paragraph Writing
A paragraph is one idea, fully explained.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Paragraph Writing

Paragraph Writing is the focus of this Writing Fundamentals lesson. It develops the learner's ability to write clear, organized, and accurate texts.

coherence

The clear and logical progression of ideas.

revision

Improvement of meaning, structure, and language after drafting.

proofreading

A final check for grammar, spelling, and punctuation.

A paragraph is a group of related sentences that develop a single main idea. It usually begins with a topic sentence, followed by supporting sentences that explain or give examples, and ends with a closing sentence.

Keep each paragraph focused on one idea. When you move to a new idea, start a new paragraph.

Steps

  1. Write a topic sentence stating the main idea.
  2. Add two to four sentences that explain or support it.
  3. Include an example or detail for proof.
  4. Use linking words: for example, also, therefore.
  5. End with a sentence that wraps up the idea.

Example

Learning English opens many doors. It helps you find better jobs in Liberia and abroad. For example, most offices require written reports in English. Therefore, strong English skills improve your future.

Why this matters

Reports, essays, and letters are all built from paragraphs. Well-organised paragraphs help readers follow your thinking, which is essential for good grades and clear professional communication.

lessons.title: 📝 Practice: Paragraph Writing
lessons.html: Quick check: Review the notes and complete the two exercises, then answer these to confirm you understood Paragraph Writing.

options: To state the main idea the paragraph will develop
questions.explanation: The topic sentence introduces the central idea that the rest of the paragraph supports and develops.

questions.question: Which quality describes a well-written, unified paragraph?
options: It covers as many different topics as possible
Every sentence relates to and supports one central idea
questions.explanation: Unity means all sentences focus on and support a single main idea, keeping the paragraph coherent.

questions.question: What role do transition words like however and therefore play in a paragraph?
options: They signal the end of the essay
They show the logical connections between ideas
questions.explanation: Transition words clarify how ideas relate to one another, improving the paragraph's flow and coherence.

lessons.title: 7.3 Essay Writing
lessons.html:
📖 Essay Writing
An essay is a guided journey through your argument.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Essay Writing

Essay Writing is the focus of this Writing Fundamentals lesson. It develops the learner's ability to write clear, organized, and accurate texts.

coherence

The clear and logical progression of ideas.

revision

Improvement of meaning, structure, and language after drafting.

proofreading

A final check for grammar, spelling, and punctuation.

An essay is a structured piece of writing that presents and develops an idea across several paragraphs. It has three main parts: an introduction that states your main idea, body paragraphs that explain and support it, and a conclusion that sums up.

A clear thesis statement in the introduction tells the reader exactly what your essay will prove.

Steps

  1. Plan your main idea and list your key points.
  2. Write an introduction ending with a clear thesis.
  3. Give each key point its own body paragraph.
  4. Support each point with reasons and examples.
  5. Write a conclusion that restates your main idea.

Example

Thesis: Youth training programmes reduce unemployment in Liberia by teaching skills, building confidence, and connecting young people to jobs. Each reason becomes one body paragraph.

Why this matters

Essays are central to exams, scholarship applications, and university study. Learning to organise a clear argument helps you think logically and persuade readers, skills valued in both school and the workplace.

lessons.html: Quick check: Review the notes and complete the two exercises, then answer these to confirm you understood Essay Writing.

options: To present the essay's main argument or central claim

questions.explanation: The thesis statement expresses the essay's central argument, guiding the whole piece.

questions.question: Which part of an essay typically restates the main argument and leaves the reader with a final thought?
questions.explanation: The conclusion restates the argument and provides a final thought, giving the essay a sense of closure.

questions.question: What is the recommended basic structure of a standard academic essay?
questions.explanation: A standard essay follows an introduction, several supporting body paragraphs, and a conclusion.

lessons.title: 7.4 Academic Writing Style
lessons.html:
📖 Academic Writing Style
Academic writing is formal, precise, and evidence-based.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Academic Writing Style

Academic Writing Style is the focus of this Writing Fundamentals lesson. It develops the learner's ability to write clear, organized, and accurate texts.

coherence

The clear and logical progression of ideas.

revision

Improvement of meaning, structure, and language after drafting.

proofreading

A final check for grammar, spelling, and punctuation.

Academic writing style is the formal way of writing used in schools, universities, and research. It is objective, uses full words instead of slang or contractions, and supports claims with evidence rather than personal feeling alone.

The tone is respectful and serious. You write to inform and prove, not to entertain or chat.

Key points

  • Use formal words: write children, not kids.
  • Avoid contractions: write do not, not don't.
  • Stay objective; avoid I feel in favour of evidence.
  • Support claims with facts, data, or sources.
  • Keep language clear, not showy or slangy.

Example

Informal: Kids don't like boring lessons. Academic: Research suggests that learners engage more when lessons are interactive.

Why this matters

Lecturers, examiners, and professional readers expect a formal style. Mastering it helps you succeed in coursework, research reports, and official documents, and it makes your writing credible and respected.

options: To maintain a formal, objective, and professional tone
Because they take up too much space

questions.explanation: Avoiding contractions and slang keeps the tone formal and objective, as academic conventions require.

questions.question: In academic writing, why are claims typically supported with citations?
options: To give credit to sources and strengthen credibility
questions.explanation: Citations credit the original sources and lend authority and credibility to the writer's claims.

lessons.title: 7.5 Writing Clearly and Concisely
lessons.html:
📖 Writing Clearly and Concisely
Say more with fewer, well-chosen words.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Writing Clearly and Concisely

Writing Clearly and Concisely is the focus of this Writing Fundamentals lesson. It develops the learner's ability to write clear, organized, and accurate texts.

coherence

The clear and logical progression of ideas.

revision

Improvement of meaning, structure, and language after drafting.

proofreading

A final check for grammar, spelling, and punctuation.

Writing clearly and concisely means expressing your ideas in a way that is easy to understand, using no more words than necessary. Clear writing removes confusion; concise writing removes waste.

Long, crowded sentences tire the reader. Short, direct sentences carry the meaning straight to the point.

Steps

  1. Decide your main point before you write.
  2. Prefer simple words over big, complicated ones.
  3. Cut repeated ideas and empty phrases.
  4. Break long sentences into shorter ones.
  5. Read it back and delete words you do not need.

Example

Wordy: Due to the fact that it was raining, we made the decision to postpone the meeting. Clear: Because it was raining, we postponed the meeting.

Why this matters

Busy employers and readers value writing they can grasp quickly. Clear, concise emails and reports save everyone time and make you look organised, thoughtful, and professional.

lessons.title: 📝 Practice: Writing Clearly and Concisely
lessons.html: Quick check: Review the notes and complete the two exercises, then answer these to confirm you understood Writing Clearly and Concisely.

questions.question: Which revision makes the sentence more concise without losing meaning?
options: Due to the fact that it was raining, we stayed inside.

Owing to the circumstance of rain, we did not go outside.
questions.explanation: Replacing the wordy phrase due to the fact that with because keeps the meaning while removing clutter.

questions.question: Why is the active voice often preferred over the passive voice for clear writing?
options: It is grammatically required in all sentences
It hides who performs the action
It usually makes sentences more direct and easier to follow
questions.explanation: The active voice states clearly who does what, making sentences more direct and readable.

questions.question: Which practice best supports concise writing?
options: Cutting unnecessary words and redundant phrases
Repeating the main idea in several ways
Adding as many adjectives as possible
questions.explanation: Removing redundant words and filler tightens the writing and makes the meaning clearer.

lessons.title: 7.6 Editing and Proofreading
lessons.html:
📖 Editing and Proofreading
First drafts are for ideas; editing makes them shine.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Editing and Proofreading

Editing and Proofreading is the focus of this Writing Fundamentals lesson. It develops the learner's ability to write clear, organized, and accurate texts.

coherence

The clear and logical progression of ideas.

revision

Improvement of meaning, structure, and language after drafting.

proofreading

A final check for grammar, spelling, and punctuation.

Editing and proofreading are the steps you take to improve and correct your writing before sharing it. Editing improves the content and flow of ideas; proofreading catches small errors in spelling, grammar, and punctuation.

No good writer skips this stage. Even short emails deserve a quick second look.

Steps

  1. Take a short break, then reread your work fresh.
  2. Edit first: check that ideas are clear and ordered.
  3. Proofread next: check spelling and punctuation.
  4. Read aloud to catch missing or repeated words.
  5. Check names, dates, and numbers are correct.

Example

Before: i will send the repot to you tommorow. After proofreading: I will send the report to you tomorrow.

Why this matters

Errors in a job application or business letter can cost you an opportunity. Careful editing and proofreading show that you are professional, detail-oriented, and someone whose work can be trusted.

lessons.title: 📝 Practice: Editing and Proofreading
lessons.html: Quick check: Review the notes and complete the two exercises, then answer these to confirm you understood Editing and Proofreading.

questions.question: What is the main difference between editing and proofreading?
options: They are exactly the same task

Editing only fixes commas, while proofreading rewrites ideas

questions.explanation: Editing focuses on content, clarity, and structure, whereas proofreading targets final surface errors like spelling and punctuation.

questions.question: Why is it helpful to read your writing aloud during proofreading?
options: It replaces the need to check spelling
It helps you catch awkward phrasing and missing words
It is only useful for poetry
questions.explanation: Reading aloud makes awkward sentences and omitted words easier to notice than silent reading.

questions.question: Which of the following is a proofreading task rather than an editing task?
options: Correcting a misspelled word and a missing comma
questions.explanation: Fixing spelling and punctuation are surface corrections, which is the core work of proofreading.

lessons.title: 8.1 Research Essays
lessons.html:
📖 Research Essays
A research essay lets your evidence do the arguing.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Research Essays

Research Essays is the focus of this Academic Writing lesson. It develops the learner's ability to produce ethical academic work supported by reliable sources.

thesis

The central claim or controlling idea of an academic text.

source

A work from which information or evidence is obtained.

citation

Formal acknowledgment of borrowed information or ideas.

A research essay is an extended piece of academic writing that answers a question by gathering evidence from reliable sources, analysing it, and building a clear argument. Unlike a personal opinion piece, every major claim is supported by cited facts, data, or expert views.

A good essay has a thesis (your main argument), body paragraphs that each develop one idea, and a conclusion that ties everything together.

Steps

  1. Choose a focused topic and turn it into a clear research question.
  2. Gather sources: books, journals, and credible websites. Take organised notes.
  3. Write a thesis statement stating your position.
  4. Draft an outline: introduction, body points, conclusion.
  5. Write body paragraphs, each with a topic sentence and cited evidence.
  6. Revise for logic, then edit grammar and check every citation.

Example

Thesis: Expanding rural internet access in Liberia would raise secondary-school pass rates, because studies show digital learning tools improve exam performance (Kollie, 2022).

Why this matters

University and workplace tasks constantly ask you to research, take a position, and defend it with evidence. Mastering the research essay trains the reasoning employers and lecturers value most.

lessons.title: 📝 Practice: Research Essays
lessons.html: Quick check: Review the notes and complete the two exercises, then answer these to confirm you understood Research Essays.

questions.question: What is the primary purpose of a thesis statement in a research essay?
options: To state the essay's central argument or claim
To list every source consulted during research
To summarize the conclusion in advance
To provide background facts about the topic
questions.explanation: A thesis statement expresses the essay's main argument that the rest of the paper supports.

questions.question: Which section of a research essay presents evidence and analysis to support the argument?
questions.explanation: Body paragraphs develop and support the thesis with evidence and analysis.

questions.question: Why should a research essay use credible, peer-reviewed sources?
options: To strengthen the argument with reliable evidence
To replace the need for a thesis
questions.explanation: Credible sources give the argument reliable, verifiable support that readers can trust.

lessons.title: 8.2 Reports
lessons.html:
📖 Reports
A report tells the reader what happened and what to do next.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Reports

Reports is the focus of this Academic Writing lesson. It develops the learner's ability to produce ethical academic work supported by reliable sources.

thesis

The central claim or controlling idea of an academic text.

source

A work from which information or evidence is obtained.

citation

Formal acknowledgment of borrowed information or ideas.

A report is a structured, factual document that investigates a situation and presents findings clearly. Academic reports (like lab or field reports) record methods and results; business reports analyse problems and recommend action. Both use headings so a busy reader can skim quickly.

Reports are objective and organised, moving from purpose to findings to recommendations.

Steps

  1. Define the purpose and who will read it.
  2. Gather and verify your facts, data, or observations.
  3. Draft a structure: Title, Introduction, Methods, Findings, Conclusion, Recommendations.
  4. Present findings with clear headings, tables, or charts.
  5. Base recommendations only on your findings.
  6. Add an executive summary at the top and proofread.

Example

Executive Summary: This report reviews water supply at Buchanan Market. Findings show two of five taps are broken. We recommend repairs within 30 days to restore vendor access.

Why this matters

From science labs to NGOs and government offices, reports are the standard way decisions get informed. Writing them clearly marks you as reliable and professional.

lessons.title: 📝 Practice: Reports
lessons.html: Quick check: Review the notes and complete the two exercises, then answer these to confirm you understood Reports.

questions.question: Which feature most distinguishes a report from an essay?
options: It must be written in the first person
It uses clearly labeled sections and headings
questions.explanation: Reports are organized into distinct labeled sections and headings for easy navigation.

questions.question: In a formal report, what is the main purpose of the executive summary?
options: To give a brief overview of key findings and recommendations
questions.explanation: The executive summary briefly conveys the report's key findings and recommendations for busy readers.

questions.question: Where in a report would specific advice for action typically appear?
questions.explanation: The recommendations section states the actions suggested based on the findings.

lessons.title: 8.3 Literature Reviews
lessons.html:
📖 Literature Reviews
Show what is already known before you add your own voice.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Literature Reviews

Literature Reviews is the focus of this Academic Writing lesson. It develops the learner's ability to produce ethical academic work supported by reliable sources.

thesis

The central claim or controlling idea of an academic text.

source

A work from which information or evidence is obtained.

citation

Formal acknowledgment of borrowed information or ideas.

A literature review surveys and evaluates existing research on a topic. It is not a list of summaries; it groups sources by theme, compares their findings, and points out gaps that your own work could fill.

It shows your reader that you understand the scholarly conversation you are joining.

Steps

  1. Define your topic and search for relevant, credible sources.
  2. Read and take notes on each source's main argument and method.
  3. Group sources by theme, method, or viewpoint rather than one-by-one.
  4. Write an introduction stating the scope and purpose.
  5. In the body, synthesise: compare and contrast findings across sources.
  6. Conclude by naming the gap your research will address, with full citations.

Example

While Doe (2019) links mobile banking to rural savings growth, Cooper (2021) finds weak effects without financial literacy training, revealing a gap this study explores.

Why this matters

Every thesis, grant proposal, and serious research project begins with a literature review. It proves you can read critically and position new ideas responsibly.

lessons.title: 📝 Practice: Literature Reviews
lessons.html: Quick check: Review the notes and complete the two exercises, then answer these to confirm you understood Literature Reviews.

questions.question: What is the main goal of a literature review?
options: To survey and synthesize existing research on a topic
questions.explanation: A literature review surveys and synthesizes what has already been published on a topic.

questions.question: A strong literature review does more than summarize sources by also doing what?
options: Identifying gaps, patterns, and relationships between studies
questions.explanation: A good review synthesizes sources, showing patterns, gaps, and how studies relate.

questions.question: Why is it important to organize a literature review thematically rather than source by source?
options: It shows connections between ideas rather than isolated summaries
It removes the need for citations
questions.explanation: Thematic organization reveals connections and debates across sources instead of disconnected summaries.

lessons.title: 8.4 Summaries
lessons.html:
📖 Summaries
Capture the whole idea in a fraction of the words.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Summaries

Summaries is the focus of this Academic Writing lesson. It develops the learner's ability to produce ethical academic work supported by reliable sources.

thesis

The central claim or controlling idea of an academic text.

source

A work from which information or evidence is obtained.

citation

Formal acknowledgment of borrowed information or ideas.

A summary restates the main points of a longer text in your own words, briefly and accurately. It keeps only the central ideas and leaves out examples and minor detail, staying faithful to the original author's meaning.

A strong summary is short, objective, and never adds your own opinion.

Steps

  1. Read the whole text carefully to grasp its overall message.
  2. Identify the main idea and the key supporting points.
  3. Set the text aside and note those points in your own words.
  4. Write one or two paragraphs, starting with the author and main idea.
  5. Cut examples, repetition, and detail; keep only essentials.
  6. Check that your version is accurate and shorter than the original.

Example

In her article, Sirleaf (2020) argues that small farmer cooperatives in Bong County raise incomes by sharing tools and negotiating better crop prices together.

Why this matters

Lecturers, managers, and clients rarely have time to read everything. A clear summary saves them time and shows you can identify what truly matters.

lessons.title: 📝 Practice: Summaries
lessons.html: Quick check: Review the notes and complete the two exercises, then answer these to confirm you understood Summaries.

questions.question: What is the key characteristic of an effective summary?
options: It adds the writer's new opinions
It restates only the main ideas in condensed form
It is longer than the original text
questions.explanation: A summary condenses the source to its main ideas without adding new content.

questions.question: When writing a summary, how should you treat minor details and examples?
options: Generally omit them and focus on main points
questions.explanation: Summaries focus on main points and leave out minor details and examples.

questions.question: Which practice keeps a summary faithful to the original source?
options: Changing the author's meaning to fit your view
Adding facts not in the source
Accurately representing the author's ideas in your own words
questions.explanation: A faithful summary conveys the author's actual meaning in your own words.

lessons.title: 8.5 Paraphrasing
lessons.html:
📖 Paraphrasing
Say it in your own words without losing the meaning.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Paraphrasing

Paraphrasing is the focus of this Academic Writing lesson. It develops the learner's ability to produce ethical academic work supported by reliable sources.

thesis

The central claim or controlling idea of an academic text.

source

A work from which information or evidence is obtained.

citation

Formal acknowledgment of borrowed information or ideas.

Paraphrasing means restating someone else's idea in your own words and sentence structure while keeping the original meaning. Unlike a summary, a paraphrase is usually about the same length as the source. You still credit the author with a citation.

Good paraphrasing changes the words and structure, not just a few synonyms.

Steps

  1. Read the passage until you fully understand it.
  2. Cover the original and write the idea from memory in your own words.
  3. Change both the vocabulary and the sentence structure.
  4. Compare with the original to confirm the meaning is the same.
  5. Ensure the wording is genuinely yours, not a near-copy.
  6. Add an in-text citation naming the source.

Example

Original: Rainfall in Monrovia peaks between June and September. Paraphrase: Monrovia receives most of its rain during the months from June through September (Weah, 2021).

Why this matters

Paraphrasing lets you use expert ideas smoothly in your own writing while avoiding plagiarism. It is a core skill for essays, reports, and professional documents.

lessons.title: 8.6 Referencing & Citations
lessons.html:
📖 Referencing & Citations
Give credit and let readers find your sources.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Referencing & Citations

Referencing & Citations is the focus of this Academic Writing lesson. It develops the learner's ability to produce ethical academic work supported by reliable sources.

thesis

The central claim or controlling idea of an academic text.

source

A work from which information or evidence is obtained.

citation

Formal acknowledgment of borrowed information or ideas.

A citation is a short note in your text showing where an idea came from; a reference is the full source detail listed at the end. Together they prove your claims, credit original authors, and let readers verify your work. Common styles include APA, MLA, and Harvard.

Pick one style and use it consistently throughout.

Steps

  1. Confirm which citation style your lecturer or organisation requires.
  2. Record full details of every source as you research.
  3. Add an in-text citation each time you quote or paraphrase.
  4. Match each in-text citation to a full entry in your reference list.
  5. Order the reference list alphabetically by author surname.
  6. Check punctuation, dates, and formatting against the style guide.

Example

In-text: (Toe, 2020). Reference: Toe, J. (2020). Coastal Erosion in Liberia. Monrovia: University Press.

Why this matters

Accurate referencing builds academic honesty and credibility. Employers and examiners trust writers who back up claims and respect others' work.

lessons.title: 📝 Practice: Referencing & Citations
lessons.html: Quick check: Review the notes and complete the two exercises, then answer these to confirm you understood Referencing & Citations.

options: To make the paper look longer

questions.explanation: Citations credit the original authors and allow readers to trace the sources.

questions.explanation: APA is a recognized academic citation style, unlike file or markup formats.

options: They are identical in every way
In-text citations are brief pointers; reference entries give full source details
Reference entries are shorter than in-text citations
In-text citations appear only on the title page
questions.explanation: In-text citations are brief markers, while the reference list gives complete source details.

lessons.title: 8.7 Avoiding Plagiarism
lessons.html:
📖 Avoiding Plagiarism
Use others' ideas honestly, and your work stays your own.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Avoiding Plagiarism

Avoiding Plagiarism is the focus of this Academic Writing lesson. It develops the learner's ability to produce ethical academic work supported by reliable sources.

thesis

The central claim or controlling idea of an academic text.

source

A work from which information or evidence is obtained.

citation

Formal acknowledgment of borrowed information or ideas.

Plagiarism is presenting someone else's words, ideas, or data as if they were yours. It can be deliberate copying or careless failure to cite. Whether intentional or not, it carries serious penalties in school and at work, including failed courses and lost jobs.

The cure is simple: always give credit and always write in your own voice.

Steps

  1. Take clear notes that mark which ideas are quotes and which are yours.
  2. Put any exact wording inside quotation marks and cite it.
  3. Paraphrase properly, changing words and structure, then cite the source.
  4. Cite ideas, statistics, and images, not just direct quotes.
  5. Keep a running reference list of every source used.
  6. Run a plagiarism check or reread before submitting.

Example

Weak: Digital tools improve learning. Honest: Digital tools improve learning outcomes in rural schools (Kollie, 2022).

Why this matters

Integrity is the foundation of academic and professional trust. Learning to credit sources protects your reputation and strengthens your arguments.

lessons.title: 📝 Practice: Avoiding Plagiarism

questions.question: Which action best helps you avoid plagiarism?
options: Using only one source for the whole paper

questions.explanation: Properly citing all borrowed ideas, words, and data prevents plagiarism.

questions.question: When you use an author's exact words, what must you do?
options: Change one word so it counts as yours
Leave them uncited if they are short
Put them in quotation marks and cite the source
questions.explanation: Exact wording requires quotation marks and a citation to avoid plagiarism.

questions.question: Why is self-plagiarism a concern in academic work?
options: Reusing your own previous work without disclosure can be dishonest
It is encouraged to save time
questions.explanation: Submitting your own prior work as new without disclosure is a form of academic dishonesty.

lessons.title: 9.1 Business Emails
lessons.html:
📖 Business Emails
A clear email can open doors a phone call cannot.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Business Emails

Business Emails is the focus of this Professional Writing lesson. It develops the learner's ability to create professional workplace documents that achieve a clear purpose.

professional tone

Respectful, clear language appropriate for work.

format

The conventional arrangement of a document.

call to action

A clear statement of what the reader should do next.

A business email is a short, professional message sent for work purposes: requests, updates, or replies. It is more formal than a text, with a clear subject line, a polite greeting, a focused message, and a proper sign-off.

Busy readers appreciate emails that state the purpose early and keep to the point.

Steps

  1. Write a specific subject line so the reader knows the topic.
  2. Open with a professional greeting using the person's name and title.
  3. State your purpose in the first sentence.
  4. Give the key details in short paragraphs or bullet points.
  5. Close with a clear request or next step.
  6. Sign off politely and add your name and contact details.

Example

Subject: Request for Meeting on Thursday. Dear Mr. Gbla, I am writing to request a short meeting to discuss the training schedule. Would Thursday at 10 a.m. suit you? Kind regards, Grace Wilson.

Why this matters

Email is the main channel of professional communication across Liberia and beyond. A well-written email builds your credibility and gets faster, better responses.

lessons.title: 9.2 Letters
lessons.html:
📖 Letters
A formal letter carries weight that a quick message never will.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Letters

Letters is the focus of this Professional Writing lesson. It develops the learner's ability to create professional workplace documents that achieve a clear purpose.

professional tone

Respectful, clear language appropriate for work.

format

The conventional arrangement of a document.

call to action

A clear statement of what the reader should do next.

A formal letter is a structured written document used for official communication such as applications, complaints, or requests. It follows a set layout with sender and recipient addresses, a date, a salutation, body paragraphs, and a formal closing.

Letters remain the standard for official records at banks, schools, and government offices.

Steps

  1. Place your address and the date at the top.
  2. Add the recipient's name, title, and address.
  3. Open with a formal salutation, such as Dear Madam.
  4. State your purpose in the first paragraph.
  5. Give supporting details in the middle paragraphs.
  6. Close politely with Yours faithfully or Yours sincerely, then sign your name.

Example

Dear Sir, I am writing to apply for the position of office assistant advertised in the Daily Observer on 5 August 2026. Please find my CV attached.

Why this matters

Formal letters create official records and make strong first impressions. Knowing the correct layout shows respect and professionalism in any serious dealing.

lessons.title: 9.3 Memorandums
lessons.html:
📖 Memorandums
One short memo can align a whole office.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Memorandums

Memorandums is the focus of this Professional Writing lesson. It develops the learner's ability to create professional workplace documents that achieve a clear purpose.

professional tone

Respectful, clear language appropriate for work.

format

The conventional arrangement of a document.

call to action

A clear statement of what the reader should do next.

A memorandum, or memo, is a brief internal document used to share information, instructions, or decisions within an organisation. It is less formal than a letter and skips addresses, using a simple header instead: To, From, Date, and Subject.

Memos are direct and focus on one clear message.

Steps

  1. Fill in the header: To, From, Date, and Subject.
  2. Open with a sentence stating the memo's purpose.
  3. Give the necessary details clearly, using bullets for lists.
  4. State any action required and the deadline.
  5. Keep it short: one page is usually enough.
  6. Reread to ensure the message is clear and professional.

Example

To: All Staff. From: HR Office. Date: 13 August 2026. Subject: Office Closure. Please note the office will close early at 2 p.m. on Friday for maintenance. Plan your work accordingly.

Why this matters

Memos keep teams informed and coordinated. Writing clear, concise memos shows you can communicate efficiently within any organisation.

lessons.title: 9.4 Meeting Minutes
lessons.html:
📖 Meeting Minutes
Minutes turn a conversation into a record everyone can trust.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Meeting Minutes

Meeting Minutes is the focus of this Professional Writing lesson. It develops the learner's ability to create professional workplace documents that achieve a clear purpose.

professional tone

Respectful, clear language appropriate for work.

format

The conventional arrangement of a document.

call to action

A clear statement of what the reader should do next.

Meeting minutes are the official written record of what happened in a meeting: who attended, what was discussed, what was decided, and who is responsible for each action. They are factual and neutral, not a word-for-word transcript.

Good minutes let absent members follow decisions and hold people accountable.

Steps

  1. Record the meeting title, date, time, and attendees.
  2. Note apologies from those absent.
  3. List each agenda item as it is discussed.
  4. Summarise key points, decisions, and votes for each item.
  5. Record action items with the responsible person and deadline.
  6. Note the next meeting date and circulate the minutes promptly.

Example

Item 3: Budget. The committee approved US$500 for supplies. Action: Mr. Toe to purchase materials by 20 August 2026.

Why this matters

Committees, NGOs, and businesses rely on minutes to track decisions and responsibilities. Accurate minutes prevent disputes and keep projects moving.

lessons.title: 9.5 Reports
lessons.html:
📖 Reports
The business report: findings a busy manager can act on.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Reports

Reports is the focus of this Professional Writing lesson. It develops the learner's ability to create professional workplace documents that achieve a clear purpose.

professional tone

Respectful, clear language appropriate for work.

format

The conventional arrangement of a document.

call to action

A clear statement of what the reader should do next.

Module 8 covered the academic report, where method and evidence lead. A workplace report is written for someone who will decide something, and it is organised for that.

The most important difference is that recommendations come early. An executive summary at the top states the finding and the recommended action, so a reader who stops after a paragraph still has what they need.

Steps

  1. Start with an executive summary: the finding and the recommendation.
  2. State the purpose and who asked for the report.
  3. Present findings with headings a reader can skim.
  4. Separate fact from interpretation clearly.
  5. Make recommendations specific, with an owner and a date.
  6. Keep it as short as the decision allows.

Why this matters

A workplace report that buries its recommendation on page four does not get acted on. Leading with the decision is what makes it useful rather than merely accurate.

lessons.title: 9.6 Proposals
lessons.html:
📖 Proposals
A strong proposal turns an idea into approved action.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Proposals

Proposals is the focus of this Professional Writing lesson. It develops the learner's ability to create professional workplace documents that achieve a clear purpose.

professional tone

Respectful, clear language appropriate for work.

format

The conventional arrangement of a document.

call to action

A clear statement of what the reader should do next.

A proposal is a persuasive document that suggests a plan and asks the reader to approve it, whether it is a project, a service, or funding. It explains the problem, offers a solution, and shows the benefits and costs clearly.

Proposals combine facts with persuasion to win support and resources.

Steps

  1. Identify the problem or need you want to address.
  2. State your proposed solution and its main goal.
  3. Explain how you will carry it out, step by step.
  4. Outline the resources, budget, and timeline required.
  5. Highlight the benefits and expected results.
  6. End with a clear request for approval and proofread carefully.

Example

Problem: Youth in Paynesville lack computer skills. Solution: A three-month training centre serving 60 students. Requested funding: US$4,000. Outcome: Improved job readiness.

Why this matters

Whether seeking a grant, pitching a business, or launching a project, proposals are how ideas get funded and approved. Persuasive, well-structured proposals open real opportunities.

lessons.title: 9.7 Resume (CV) Writing

📖 Resume (CV) Writing
Your CV is your first interview, done on paper.

Key Words & Meanings

call to action

A resume, or CV, is a concise summary of your qualifications, experience, and skills used to apply for jobs. It gives an employer a quick, organised picture of what you offer and why you fit the role.

A strong CV is clear, honest, tailored to the job, and free of errors.

Steps

  1. Start with your name and contact details at the top.
  2. Add a short professional summary of who you are.
  3. List work experience, most recent first, with dates and achievements.
  4. Include education and relevant qualifications.
  5. Add key skills, languages, and references.
  6. Tailor it to each job and proofread for spelling and layout.

Example

Sales Assistant, Kollie Stores, Monrovia (2023 to 2025): Served 40+ customers daily and increased weekly sales by 15 percent through friendly service.

Why this matters

A well-written CV decides whether you get an interview at all. In a competitive job market, a clear, professional CV sets you apart from other applicants.

lessons.title: 9.8 Cover Letters

📖 Cover Letters
The letter that makes your resume come alive.

Key Words & Meanings

A cover letter is a short, personalised letter you send with your resume. While the resume lists facts, the cover letter tells a small story about why you are the right person and why you want this particular job.

It should be one page, addressed to a real person where possible, and tailored to the specific role.

Steps

  1. Open with the exact job title you are applying for.
  2. State briefly why you are interested in the company.
  3. Give one or two examples that match the job requirements.
  4. Explain what you will contribute to the team.
  5. Close politely and thank the reader.

Example

"Dear Mr. Kollie, I am applying for the Customer Service Officer role at LibTelco. During two years at a busy Monrovia phone shop, I handled over 30 customers daily and resolved complaints calmly. I would bring that same patience to your team."

Why this matters

A thoughtful cover letter shows respect and effort. It proves you can write professionally and connect your experience to an employer's needs, helping you stand out among many applicants with similar resumes.

lessons.title: 10.2 Creating Presentation Slides
lessons.html:
📖 Creating Presentation Slides
Good slides support your words; they do not replace them.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Creating Presentation Slides

Creating Presentation Slides is the focus of this Presentation & Public Speaking lesson. It develops the learner's ability to design and deliver confident, audience-focused presentations.

signpost

Language guiding an audience through a presentation.

visual aid

A slide, chart, or image supporting spoken ideas.

delivery

The use of voice, pace, expression, and body language.

Presentation slides are visual aids that help your audience follow your main ideas. In academic and professional English, effective slides are simple, clear, and easy to read from the back of a room. Each slide should carry one main idea, not a wall of text.

Use short bullet points, large fonts, and a few strong images or charts. You are the presenter; the slides only guide the listener.

Steps

  1. Plan your key message before opening any software.
  2. Give each slide one clear heading and one main point.
  3. Use bullets of five words or fewer, not full sentences.
  4. Choose a large, plain font and strong colour contrast.
  5. Add one relevant image or chart per idea.
  6. Practise reading each slide aloud in about thirty seconds.

Example

A student in Monrovia presenting on clean water uses a slide titled "Why Clean Water Matters" with three bullets: Health, School attendance, Farm income. A photo of a village well fills the side. She speaks the details; the slide only reminds the audience.

Why this matters

Clear slides make you look organised and professional in class presentations, job pitches, and team meetings. Audiences trust speakers whose visuals are easy to follow, and clean slides help you win support for your ideas.

lessons.title: 📝 Practice: Creating Presentation Slides
lessons.html: Quick check: Review the notes and complete the two exercises, then answer these to confirm you understood Creating Presentation Slides.

questions.question: What is the best practice for the amount of text on a single presentation slide?
options: Fill the slide with full paragraphs so nothing is forgotten
Use a few short bullet points or key phrases
Write the entire speech word for word

questions.explanation: Slides should support the speaker with concise key points, not replace the spoken words with dense text.

questions.question: Which choice would most improve the readability of a slide for a large room?

lessons.title: 10.3 Speaking with Confidence
lessons.html:
📖 Speaking with Confidence
Confidence is a skill you build, not a gift you are born with.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Speaking with Confidence

Speaking with Confidence is the focus of this Presentation & Public Speaking lesson. It develops the learner's ability to design and deliver confident, audience-focused presentations.

signpost

Language guiding an audience through a presentation.

visual aid

A slide, chart, or image supporting spoken ideas.

delivery

The use of voice, pace, expression, and body language.

Speaking with confidence means delivering your message clearly, at a steady pace, and with a strong voice so your audience believes and follows you. Nervousness is normal, but preparation and practice turn nerves into energy.

Confident speakers control their breathing, pause on purpose, and speak loudly enough for everyone to hear.

Steps

  1. Prepare well so you know your material deeply.
  2. Take a slow, deep breath before you begin.
  3. Speak slightly slower than feels natural to you.
  4. Use short pauses instead of fillers like er and em.
  5. Project your voice to reach the back of the room.
  6. Make eye contact with friendly faces to steady yourself.

Example

Before a job interview in Accra, Grace pauses, breathes, and opens: "Good morning. My name is Grace Doe, and I am here to share why I am the right fit for this role." Her steady voice and calm pace signal confidence at once.

Why this matters

In interviews, class defences, and workplace meetings, people judge your ideas partly by how you deliver them. Confident speaking helps your knowledge come across clearly and earns the respect of teachers, employers, and colleagues.

📖 Body Language

Body language is the messages you send through posture, gestures, facial expression, and eye contact. In professional English, strong body language supports your words and shows that you are confident, honest, and engaged.

Standing tall, facing your audience, and using open hands make you appear trustworthy and in control.

Key points

  • Stand straight with shoulders relaxed, not slouched.
  • Keep your arms open, avoiding crossed or hidden hands.
  • Use natural gestures to stress important points.
  • Make eye contact across the whole audience, not one spot.
  • Smile warmly to build a friendly connection.
  • Avoid nervous habits like fidgeting or turning away.

Example

During a community health talk, Moses stands upright, spreads his hands as he says "We can all help," and looks slowly around the room. His open posture makes villagers feel included and willing to listen.

Why this matters

Audiences read your body before they weigh your words. Strong body language makes presentations, interviews, and meetings more persuasive, while poor posture or closed gestures can make even good ideas seem weak or dishonest.

📖 Audience Engagement
A speech is a conversation, not a lecture at a wall.

Audience engagement means keeping your listeners active, interested, and involved throughout your presentation. Engaged audiences remember more and support your ideas. You achieve this by inviting attention, not just delivering facts.

Questions, stories, and eye contact turn passive listeners into active partners.

Steps

  1. Open with a question or short story that grabs interest.
  2. Use names, local examples, and relatable situations.
  3. Ask the audience simple questions during your talk.
  4. Invite a show of hands or a quick response.
  5. Vary your voice and pace to hold attention.
  6. Watch faces and adjust if people look lost or bored.

Example

Opening a training in Freetown, Fatu asks, "By a show of hands, who has waited too long for a bus this week?" Hands rise, people laugh, and she connects the problem to her topic on transport planning.

Why this matters

Whether teaching, pitching, or reporting at work, an engaged audience listens, understands, and acts on your message. Engagement skills help students pass oral defences and help professionals win clients, funding, and cooperation.

lessons.title: 10.6 Handling Questions

📖 Handling Questions
A good answer can matter more than the whole speech.
